section-117: The term 'Northeast' as a single region is a modern, largely postcolonial category, now covering eight states: Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, Tripura, Meghalaya and Sikkim (added to the North Eastern Council in 2002). Before colonial rule, the area contained independent kingdoms (the Ahoms, Kacharis, Jaintias, Koches, Manipur, Tripura) and many self-governing hill communities with links to Bengal, Tibet, Myanmar and Yunnan.

Historians such as Sanjib Baruah ('Durable Disorder', 'In the Name of the Nation') and Gunnel Cederlöf argue that the region was 'made' by colonial frontier policy, the Partition of 1947 and postcolonial state-building. The region is connected to the rest of India only by the narrow Siliguri Corridor ('chicken's neck', about 22 km wide). About 98 percent of its borders are international - with China, Myanmar, Bangladesh, Bhutan and Nepal.
section-118: After the First Anglo-Burmese War (1824-1826), the Treaty of Yandabo (24 February 1826) gave the British control of Assam, Manipur's independence (under British influence) and Arakan. The British annexed Lower Assam (1828), installed the Ahom prince Purandar Singha in Upper Assam (1833) and annexed it in 1838; they annexed Cachar (1832) and the Jaintia kingdom (1835). Khasi resistance under U Tirot Sing (1829-1833) was suppressed.

Later expeditions brought the hills under control: the Garo Hills (1872-1873), the Naga Hills (Kohima became headquarters in 1878; the Battle of Khonoma, 1879-1880), the Lushai Hills (expeditions of 1871-1872 and 1889-1890), and Manipur after the Anglo-Manipur War (1891), when Tikendrajit and Thangal General were executed, and Manipur became a princely state. Expeditions into the Abor (Adi) and Mishmi hills followed in the early twentieth century (the Abor Expedition, 1911-1912). Tea, oil (Digboi, 1889), coal and timber drove colonial interest.
section-119: The Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation of 1873 created the 'Inner Line', which prohibited British subjects (non-residents) from entering certain hill areas without a pass (the Inner Line Permit, ILP). It was originally intended to protect the commercial interests of the colonial state (tea gardens, rubber and elephant trade) from conflict with hill communities, to prevent unauthorised expansion of plantations and to control the frontier.

Areas such as the Naga Hills, Lushai Hills and the frontier tracts (later NEFA, now Arunachal Pradesh) came under the Inner Line. After independence, the ILP system was retained to protect tribal land and culture, and today it applies in Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Mizoram and Manipur (extended in 2019). Indian citizens from other states need permits to enter. It is seen as protecting indigenous identity but also criticised for isolating the region.
section-120: The British adopted a policy of 'loose political control' over the hills beyond the plains: they did not administer them directly but tried to stop raids through punitive expeditions, blockades and agreements with chiefs. The hill areas were treated differently from the plains: they were excluded from regular laws, ruled through chiefs and customary law under political officers, and isolated from nationalist politics.

The Government of India Act 1919 made them 'backward tracts', and the Government of India Act 1935 classified them as 'Excluded Areas' (such as the Naga Hills, Lushai Hills and North Cachar Hills) under the Governor's direct control, and 'Partially Excluded Areas' (such as the Garo Hills and Mikir Hills). Some British officials (Robert Reid, J. P. Mills) proposed a separate 'Crown Colony' of the hill areas (the 'Coupland Plan'), which was not implemented. These policies created distinct administrative and political identities and shaped later boundaries and demands.
section-121: Before 1947, Assam and the hills were connected to the outside world by the Brahmaputra and Barak river routes through East Bengal to Calcutta and Chittagong, by railways (the Assam-Bengal Railway to Chittagong port) and by trade routes to Burma, Tibet and Yunnan. Partition in 1947 made East Bengal into East Pakistan (Bangladesh from 1971), cutting off these routes; Sylhet district went to Pakistan after a referendum. The region became linked to India only through the Siliguri Corridor.

The closing of borders with China (especially after the 1962 war) and Myanmar also blocked historic connections. The region became landlocked and economically isolated, with higher transport costs and lost markets. Today, India's 'Act East Policy', the Kaladan project through Myanmar to Mizoram, transit agreements with Bangladesh (use of Chittagong and Mongla ports) and new road and rail links try to reconnect the region with its neighbours.
section-122: At independence, the Northeast consisted of Assam province (including the Naga Hills, Lushai Hills, Khasi-Jaintia and Garo Hills, Mikir and North Cachar Hills and NEFA), and the princely states of Manipur and Tripura, which merged with India in 1949. The Sixth Schedule (1950) created autonomous district councils. Demands for separate states led to reorganisation: Nagaland became a state in 1963; under the North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act 1971, Meghalaya (an autonomous state from 1970), Manipur and Tripura became full states in 1972, and Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh (formerly NEFA) became Union Territories in 1972 and states in 1987. Sikkim joined India in 1975.

The North Eastern Council (1971) was set up for regional planning, and the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER) was created in 2001. Within Assam, autonomous councils (Bodoland Territorial Council, 2003) followed. The 'breakup of Assam' reflected the assertion of tribal identities and resentment against Assamese dominance, including the imposition of Assamese as official language (1960).
section-123: The region borders China (Tibet), Bhutan, Myanmar, Bangladesh and Nepal. China claims most of Arunachal Pradesh as 'South Tibet', rejecting the McMahon Line drawn at the Simla Convention (1914) between British India and Tibet; the 1962 Sino-Indian War saw Chinese forces advance to Tezpur's outskirts before withdrawing. Insurgent groups have used bases in Myanmar, Bangladesh and Bhutan (Bhutan's 'Operation All Clear' against ULFA and others in 2003).

The region's geopolitical importance includes its role as a gateway to Southeast Asia under the Act East Policy, its rivers (the Brahmaputra flows from Tibet, raising concerns about Chinese dams), the movement of people across porous borders (such as refugees from Myanmar after the 2021 coup arriving in Mizoram) and issues of drug trafficking through the 'Golden Triangle'. Sanjib Baruah describes the region as being at the periphery of the Indian state but central to its security concerns.
section-124: The Ahoms were a Tai (Shan) people. Under their leader Sukapha (Siu-Ka-Pha), they crossed the Patkai hills from the Shan state of Mong Mao (in present Yunnan-Myanmar border region) and entered the Brahmaputra valley in 1228, establishing their kingdom with Charaideo as an early capital. They defeated or absorbed the Morans, Borahis, Chutiyas and Kacharis and gradually extended their rule over the Brahmaputra valley. 2 December is celebrated as 'Sukapha Divas' or 'Asom Divas'.

The Ahoms ruled for about 600 years (until 1826), longer than almost any other dynasty in India. They resisted repeated Mughal invasions; Lachit Borphukan defeated the Mughals at the naval Battle of Saraighat (1671). Their administration used the paik system (compulsory labour service by adult males organised in khels). They gradually adopted Hinduism (especially from the seventeenth century) and the Assamese language, while writing chronicles called buranjis in Ahom and later Assamese. Burmese invasions (1817-1826) ended their rule.
section-125: Northeast India is home to over 200 ethnic groups and many languages belonging to the Tibeto-Burman, Austroasiatic (Khasi, Pnar), Indo-Aryan (Assamese, Bengali) and Tai (Ahom, Khamti) families. Major groups include the Assamese, Bodos, Karbis, Dimasas, Mishings and Rabhas in Assam; the Khasis, Jaintias (Pnar) and Garos in Meghalaya; Nagas (over a dozen major tribes including Angami, Ao, Sema, Konyak, Lotha) in Nagaland and Manipur; Meiteis, Kukis and Nagas in Manipur; Mizos (Lusei, Hmar, Lai, Mara, Paite) in Mizoram; Tripuris, Reangs (Brus) and Bengalis in Tripura; and Adis, Nyishis, Apatanis, Monpas, Mishmis and others in Arunachal; Lepchas, Bhutias and Nepalis in Sikkim.

Sociocultural characteristics include shifting cultivation (jhum) in the hills and wet-rice farming in valleys; clan-based social organisation; village councils and chieftainship; the matrilineal systems of the Khasis and Garos, where descent and property pass through women (the youngest daughter, khadduh, inherits among the Khasis); youth dormitories (the Naga morung, Mizo zawlbuk, Adi dere and the Garo nokpante); and rich traditions of weaving, dance and festivals. The plains have Hindu and Muslim communities, the hills largely Christian communities, and Buddhism in parts of Arunachal and Sikkim.
section-126: Missionaries combined evangelism with education and medicine. The American Baptist Mission worked in Assam (from 1836, at Sadiya and later Sibsagar, publishing the first Assamese newspaper 'Orunodoi', 1846), among the Garos and Nagas (the first converts among the Ao Nagas in 1872 through E. W. Clark). The Welsh Presbyterian Mission worked among the Khasis (Thomas Jones, 1841, who introduced the Roman script for Khasi) and Mizos (from 1897).

Medical missions established hospitals such as the Welsh Mission Hospital in Shillong (1922), the Durtlang hospital in Mizoram (1928) and the Christian hospital at Serkawn (Lunglei), the Jorhat Christian Medical Centre and the Clark Memorial Hospital at Impur (Nagaland). They fought epidemics such as smallpox, cholera, malaria and kala-azar, trained local nurses, and reduced dependence on traditional sacrifices for healing. This contributed to conversion, literacy and new ideas of hygiene, but also to the decline of traditional practices.
section-127: Colonial conquest involved punitive expeditions, burning of villages and destruction of granaries, the imprisonment or exile of chiefs, and the imposition of house tax and forced labour. It transformed political authority: independent chiefs became intermediaries of colonial administration, the Ahom and Jaintia kingdoms ended, and Manipur became a princely state under British supervision.

Colonisation also brought economic change - tea plantations in Assam (from 1839), using indentured 'coolie' labour from Chotanagpur and central India under harsh conditions; oil (Digboi), coal and timber extraction; and migration of peasants from East Bengal and of traders. Plains Assam was integrated into the colonial economy while the hills were kept apart under the Inner Line and excluded-area policies. This created divisions between hills and plains and new ethnic consciousness, which shaped later politics.
section-128: Northeast India has a great variety of dances. Examples include the Bihu dance of Assam (performed during Rongali Bihu in April, celebrating the new year and spring); the Sattriya dance of the Vaishnava sattras founded by Srimanta Sankardeva, recognised as one of India's classical dances (2000); Manipuri dance, including the Ras Lila, another classical form; the Thang-ta martial art and Lai Haraoba festival dances of Manipur; Cheraw (bamboo dance) of Mizoram; the Wangala dance of the Garos; the Nongkrem and Shad Suk Mynsiem dances of the Khasis; the war dances of the Nagas; the Hojagiri dance of the Reangs of Tripura; the Bagurumba dance of the Bodos; and the Losar and Cham (masked) dances of the Monpas and Sikkim's Buddhists.

Dances are linked to agriculture (sowing and harvest), religion, warfare, life-cycle rites and community festivals. They express identity, memory and social values and are now also performed at cultural festivals such as the Hornbill Festival of Nagaland (from 2000) and Chapchar Kut of Mizoram.
section-129: Rice is the staple across the region. Food cultures reflect local ecology - forests, rivers and hills - and emphasise boiling, steaming, smoking and fermenting rather than heavy spices and oil. Common elements include fermented bamboo shoot, fermented fish (ngari in Manipur), fermented soybean (axone or akhuni in Nagaland, bekang in Mizoram, tungrymbai in Meghalaya), smoked pork, and the use of bhut jolokia (ghost chilli). Rice beer (apong, zu, judima, zutho) has ritual and social importance in many communities.

Dishes include khar and masor tenga (Assam), eromba and singju (Manipur), jadoh (Meghalaya), bai and sawhchiar (Mizoram), smoked pork with bamboo shoot (Nagaland), and thukpa and momos (Sikkim and Arunachal). Food is linked to festivals, feasts, hospitality and identity. Historians note how colonialism, Christianity, migration and markets have changed food habits, and how 'Northeast food' has become a marker of identity, sometimes facing discrimination in other Indian cities.
section-130: Naga: the Naga National Council (NNC) under A. Z. Phizo declared independence on 14 August 1947 and held a 'plebiscite' (1951); armed struggle followed, and the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act (AFSPA, 1958) was enacted. Nagaland became a state (1963); the Shillong Accord (1975) was rejected by some, who formed the NSCN (1980), which split into NSCN (IM) and NSCN (K) in 1988. A ceasefire (1997) and the Framework Agreement (2015) with NSCN (IM) have not yet produced a final settlement. Mizo: the MNF uprising (1966) and the Peace Accord (1986) leading to statehood.

Manipur: groups such as the UNLF (1964), PLA and others demanded independence; AFSPA and incidents of human rights abuse led to protests (Irom Sharmila's sixteen-year hunger strike, 2000-2016). Ethnic conflict between Meiteis and Kukis broke out in May 2023. Assam: the United Liberation Front of Asom (ULFA, 1979) sought a sovereign Assam; Bodo movements led to accords in 1993, 2003 (creating the Bodoland Territorial Council) and 2020. Tripura: the Tripura National Volunteers and later the NLFT, with an accord in 1988. Causes include identity and fears of assimilation, perceived neglect, migration and land issues, underdevelopment and the use of military force; solutions have included accords, autonomy and development.
section-131: Boundaries drawn by the British for administrative convenience, often without regard to traditional lands, became state boundaries after reorganisation. Assam has disputes with Nagaland (over areas in Golaghat, Jorhat and Sivasagar; violent clashes at Merapani in 1985), Meghalaya (twelve areas; an agreement in March 2022 settled six), Arunachal Pradesh (the Namsai Declaration of 2022 aimed at resolution) and Mizoram.

The Assam-Mizoram dispute arises from two colonial notifications: the 1875 Inner Line boundary of the Lushai Hills (based on the Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation), which Mizoram accepts as it was drawn with consultation of Mizo chiefs, and the 1933 notification demarcating the Lushai Hills and Manipur and later Cachar boundaries, which Assam follows. Clashes occurred repeatedly, most seriously on 26 July 2021 at Vairengte-Lailapur, where six Assam police personnel and a civilian were killed. Negotiations and central mediation continue.
section-132: Migration has deep roots: colonial tea planters brought over a million labourers from Chotanagpur, Odisha and central India (the 'tea tribes' or Adivasis of Assam); peasants from East Bengal (especially Mymensingh) settled in the Brahmaputra valley from the early twentieth century, encouraged by the colonial government (the 'Line System' of 1920 attempted to restrict them to certain areas); Marwari traders, Nepali graziers and Bihari labourers also came. After Partition and the Bangladesh war (1971), large numbers of refugees arrived.

Fear of demographic change led to the Assam Movement (1979-1985) led by the All Assam Students' Union (AASU) against 'illegal immigrants', culminating in the Assam Accord (15 August 1985), which fixed 24 March 1971 as the cut-off date for detection and deportation. The National Register of Citizens (NRC) update in Assam (final list 2019) excluded about 19 lakh people. In Tripura, Bengali migration made the indigenous Tripuris a minority, fuelling insurgency. In Mizoram, the Bru (Reang) people fled to Tripura after 1997 ethnic violence; the 2020 agreement allowed them to settle in Tripura. The Chakma and Hajong refugees in Arunachal also raise disputes. Migration is thus central to identity politics in the region.
section-133: The Sixth Schedule (under Articles 244(2) and 275(1)) was based on the recommendations of the Bordoloi Sub-Committee of the Constituent Assembly (chaired by Gopinath Bordoloi). It applies to tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. It provides for Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) and Regional Councils with up to 30 members (of whom up to four are nominated by the Governor), elected for five years.

The councils can make laws on land, forests (other than reserved), water, shifting cultivation, village and town administration, inheritance, marriage, divorce and social customs; can set up village courts to try cases under customary law; and can collect land revenue and certain taxes. There are ten ADCs: in Assam - the Bodoland Territorial Council, Karbi Anglong and Dima Hasao; in Meghalaya - Khasi Hills, Jaintia Hills and Garo Hills; in Tripura - the Tripura Tribal Areas ADC; and in Mizoram - the Chakma, Lai and Mara ADCs. The Schedule protects tribal autonomy, but councils often face shortage of funds, overlapping powers with state governments and demands for greater autonomy.
section-134: The Tibeto-Burman family is a branch of the Sino-Tibetan language family. In Northeast India, it includes the Bodo-Garo (Bodo, Dimasa, Garo, Kokborok of Tripura, Rabha), Kuki-Chin (Mizo, Hmar, Paite, Thadou-Kuki, Lai, Mara), Naga languages (Angami, Ao, Sema, Konyak, Lotha, Tangkhul), Meitei (Manipuri), Tani (Adi, Nyishi, Apatani, Galo, Mishing), Karbi, and the Tibetic languages (Monpa, Sherdukpen, Sikkimese Bhutia, Lepcha). Many were unwritten until missionaries introduced the Roman script in the nineteenth century; Meitei uses both the Bengali script and the revived Meitei Mayek.

Other families in the region are Austroasiatic (Khasi and Pnar of Meghalaya, and Munda languages of tea-garden communities), Indo-Aryan (Assamese, Bengali, Nepali) and Tai-Kadai (Ahom, now revived, Khamti, Phake). Linguistic diversity reflects long histories of migration from the east and north. Language has been central to identity movements, such as the demand for recognition of Bodo (in the Eighth Schedule from 2003) and Manipuri (1992).
section-135: The term 'tribe' was used by colonial administrators and anthropologists to describe communities considered 'primitive' or outside caste society, often based on evolutionary ideas. Colonial ethnographies (by J. H. Hutton and J. P. Mills on the Nagas, Shakespear on the Lushais, Gurdon on the Khasis) classified tribes. Constitutionally, 'Scheduled Tribes' (Article 342) are notified by the President based on criteria such as primitive traits, distinctive culture, geographical isolation, shyness of contact and backwardness (the Lokur Committee, 1965), which many find outdated and stigmatising.

Scholars criticise the category for homogenising diverse communities, treating them as static and isolated, and ignoring their histories, polities and interactions with states. Some prefer 'indigenous peoples' or 'Adivasi'; others note that 'tribe' has become a basis for rights, protections and political identity (Scheduled Tribe status, Sixth Schedule). In the Northeast, many communities identify proudly with their tribal identity while rejecting colonial stereotypes.
section-137: Historical geography: before the British, the region had powerful states (the Ahom kingdom in the Brahmaputra valley, the Kachari, Jaintia, Koch, Manipur and Tripura kingdoms) and autonomous hill communities, with connections to Bengal, Tibet, Burma and Yunnan through trade and migration. Colonial transformation: the Treaty of Yandabo (1826) led to the annexation of Assam (1828-1838), Cachar (1832) and Jaintia (1835); expeditions conquered the Garo, Naga and Lushai Hills; and Manipur came under British control (1891). Tea, oil and timber drove expansion.

Frontier policies: the Inner Line (1873) separated the hills from the plains; the hills were ruled through chiefs and customary law and later declared Backward Tracts (1919) and Excluded or Partially Excluded Areas (1935); the McMahon Line (1914) defined the border with Tibet. Partition (1947) cut the region off from East Bengal and its ports, making it landlocked except for the Siliguri Corridor.

Postcolonial reorganisation: the Sixth Schedule, the creation of Nagaland (1963), Meghalaya, Manipur and Tripura (1972), Mizoram and Arunachal (UT 1972, states 1987) and Sikkim (1975). Internal contradictions - ethnic diversity, hill-plain divisions, migration and insurgency - and the region's international borders (China, Myanmar, Bangladesh, Bhutan) make it geopolitically important. The Act East Policy seeks to transform it from a periphery into a gateway to Southeast Asia.
section-138: Ahoms: Tai people who arrived under Sukapha (1228), built a powerful kingdom with the paik system and buranji chronicles, resisted the Mughals (Saraighat, 1671), adopted Hinduism and the Assamese language, and ruled until the Burmese invasions and British annexation. Their history shows the long interaction between migrants and local communities.

People: the region's population includes Mongoloid (East Asian-related), Austroasiatic and Indo-Aryan elements, with over 200 communities speaking Tibeto-Burman, Austroasiatic, Indo-Aryan and Tai languages. Geographical distribution: plains peoples (Assamese, Bengalis, Bodos) in the valleys; hill communities (Nagas, Mizos, Khasis, Garos, Kukis, Adis, Nyishis) in the hills. Sociocultural features include clan organisation, village councils, youth dormitories (morung, zawlbuk), jhum and wet-rice cultivation, matrilineal systems among the Khasis and Garos, weaving traditions, oral literature and festivals. Religions include Hinduism (including Vaishnavism of Sankardeva), Christianity, Buddhism, Islam and indigenous faiths (such as Donyi-Polo and Seng Khasi).

Dance and food cultures (Bihu, Sattriya, Manipuri, Cheraw, Wangala, Naga war dances; fermented foods, bamboo shoots, smoked meats, rice beer) express identity, connect with the agricultural cycle and environment, and serve as markers of community. The region is therefore extremely diverse and should not be seen as homogeneous.
section-139: Colonial conquest: the British annexed Assam after 1826, conquered the hills through expeditions and established administration through deputy commissioners, political officers and chiefs. The Inner Line (1873) and exclusion policies (1935) kept the hills separate. Colonial economic exploitation through tea plantations, oil, timber and coal, and the import of labour, transformed the plains. Christian missions (American Baptists, Welsh Presbyterians, later Catholics and others) spread education, literacy in Roman script, medical care (hospitals in Shillong, Durtlang, Impur, Jorhat) and Christianity, transforming hill societies.

Insurgency: after independence, movements demanded sovereignty or autonomy - the Naga movement (NNC, NSCN; ceasefire 1997, Framework Agreement 2015), the Mizo movement (MNF, 1966-1986), Manipuri groups (UNLF, PLA), ULFA in Assam, Bodo groups and Tripuri groups. Causes included distinct identity and history, fear of assimilation and demographic change, economic neglect, land issues, the experience of colonial separation and harsh counter-insurgency, including AFSPA (1958), criticised for human rights abuses.

Responses: accords (Shillong 1975, Mizo 1986, Assam 1985, Bodo 1993/2003/2020, Tripura 1988, Karbi Anglong 2021), statehood and autonomous councils, development programmes and military operations. The Mizo Accord is often seen as the most successful. Each state's history must be studied specifically.
section-140: Border disputes: inherited from colonial boundaries and post-1947 reorganisation, they exist between Assam and Nagaland, Meghalaya, Arunachal and Mizoram. The Assam-Mizoram dispute arises from the conflicting 1875 and 1933 boundary notifications; the violent clash of July 2021 showed its seriousness. Agreements (Assam-Meghalaya 2022, Assam-Arunachal 2022/2023) have resolved some areas.

Migration: colonial tea labour, East Bengal peasant migration, Partition and 1971 refugees, and continuing cross-border migration changed demography and caused conflict - the Assam Movement and Accord (1985), the NRC (2019), Tripura's demographic change, the Bru crisis in Mizoram (1997-2020) and the Chakma-Hajong issue in Arunachal. Sixth Schedule: based on the Bordoloi Sub-Committee; provides autonomous district councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram with powers over land, forests, customs and justice, protecting tribal identity, but with limited finances.

Language and tribe: most languages of the region are Tibeto-Burman (Bodo-Garo, Kuki-Chin, Naga, Tani, Meitei), alongside Austroasiatic (Khasi), Indo-Aryan (Assamese, Bengali) and Tai. The category 'tribe', created in colonial ethnography and used in the Constitution, needs critical examination, as it has homogenising and stigmatising aspects but also provides a basis for rights and identity. These issues show how territory, identity, language and constitutional arrangements remain central to Northeast India.
section-143: Napoleon Bonaparte (1769-1821), born in Corsica, rose as a brilliant artillery officer in the Revolutionary wars (Toulon, 1793; Italian campaign, 1796-1797; Egyptian expedition, 1798). He seized power in the coup of 18 Brumaire (November 1799), became First Consul, Consul for life (1802) and Emperor (1804). His reforms included the Napoleonic Code (Civil Code, 1804), which established equality before the law, property rights and secular authority; the Concordat with the Pope (1801); the Bank of France; centralised administration through prefects; and the lycées (secondary schools).

He won great victories (Austerlitz, 1805; Jena, 1806; Wagram, 1809), dissolved the Holy Roman Empire (1806) and dominated Europe, but lost the naval battle of Trafalgar (1805) to Nelson. His Continental System (1806) tried to blockade Britain economically. The Peninsular War in Spain (1808-1814) and the disastrous invasion of Russia (1812), where the 'Grand Army' of 600,000 was destroyed, led to his defeat at Leipzig (Battle of the Nations, 1813) and exile to Elba (1814). He returned for the 'Hundred Days' but was defeated at Waterloo (18 June 1815) by Wellington and Blücher and exiled to St Helena, where he died in 1821. He spread revolutionary ideas such as legal equality and nationalism across Europe.
section-144: The Congress of Vienna (September 1814 - June 1815) was attended by the great powers: Austria (represented by Prince Klemens von Metternich, the dominant figure), Russia (Tsar Alexander I), Prussia (Hardenberg), Britain (Castlereagh) and France (Talleyrand). Its principles were legitimacy (restoring the old ruling dynasties, such as the Bourbons in France, Spain and Naples), the balance of power, compensation for the victors and containment of France.

Territorial changes: the Netherlands and Belgium were united as a buffer against France; Prussia gained the Rhineland and part of Saxony; Austria gained Lombardy and Venetia; Russia gained most of Poland (Congress Poland); Britain gained colonies (Cape Colony, Ceylon, Malta); the German Confederation of 39 states was created; Norway went to Sweden; and Switzerland's neutrality was recognised. The 'Concert of Europe' (Quadruple Alliance, later Quintuple) and the Holy Alliance maintained the settlement through congresses. It kept general peace in Europe until 1914, but it ignored nationalism and liberalism, leading to revolutions in 1820, 1830 and 1848.
section-145: After 1815, Italy was divided into several states: the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia, the Austrian-controlled Lombardy and Venetia, the Papal States, the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies (Naples and Sicily), and the duchies of Parma, Modena and Tuscany. The Risorgimento (resurgence) involved secret societies (the Carbonari), Giuseppe Mazzini's 'Young Italy' (1831) promoting a republic, and the revolutions of 1848, which failed.

Count Camillo di Cavour, Prime Minister of Piedmont under King Victor Emmanuel II, modernised Piedmont and used diplomacy: Piedmont joined the Crimean War (1855) and allied with Napoleon III of France, defeating Austria (1859; battles of Magenta and Solferino) to gain Lombardy; the central Italian states joined through plebiscites (1860). Giuseppe Garibaldi with his 'Thousand Red Shirts' conquered Sicily and Naples (1860) and handed them to Victor Emmanuel, who became King of Italy in 1861. Venetia was gained in 1866 (after Prussia defeated Austria) and Rome in 1870 (after French troops withdrew during the Franco-Prussian War), becoming the capital in 1871.
section-146: After 1815, Germany consisted of 39 states in the German Confederation, dominated by Austria. The Zollverein (customs union, 1834) under Prussia promoted economic unity. The Frankfurt Parliament of 1848-1849 offered the crown of a united Germany to the Prussian king, Frederick William IV, who refused it.

Otto von Bismarck, Prussian Minister-President from 1862, unified Germany through 'blood and iron'. He strengthened the army and fought three wars: against Denmark (1864) over Schleswig and Holstein; against Austria (Seven Weeks' War, 1866, battle of Sadowa/Königgrätz), which excluded Austria from German affairs and created the North German Confederation; and against France (Franco-Prussian War, 1870-1871), provoked by the Ems Telegram, in which France was defeated at Sedan and lost Alsace-Lorraine. The German Empire was proclaimed at the Hall of Mirrors in Versailles on 18 January 1871, with William I as Kaiser and Bismarck as Chancellor. A united Germany became the strongest power in continental Europe.
section-147: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain from about 1760 because of its coal and iron resources, capital from trade and colonies, agricultural revolution (enclosures, crop rotation) which released labour, a large domestic and colonial market, political stability, and inventions. Key inventions: in textiles - John Kay's flying shuttle (1733), James Hargreaves' spinning jenny (1764), Richard Arkwright's water frame (1769), Samuel Crompton's mule (1779), Edmund Cartwright's power loom (1785) and Eli Whitney's cotton gin (1793); in power - James Watt's improved steam engine (1769); in iron - Abraham Darby's coke smelting and Henry Cort's puddling process; and in transport - canals, George Stephenson's locomotive 'Rocket' (1829) and railways (Liverpool-Manchester, 1830) and steamships.

It spread to Belgium, France, Germany, the USA and Japan in the nineteenth century; a 'Second Industrial Revolution' (from about 1870) introduced steel, electricity, chemicals and oil. Effects: factory system, urbanisation, a working class living in poor conditions (child labour, long hours), the rise of capitalism and the middle class, trade unions, socialist ideas (Marx and Engels' 'Communist Manifesto', 1848), factory laws, imperialism to secure raw materials and markets, and environmental pollution.
section-148: The middle class (bourgeoisie) included industrialists, merchants, bankers, professionals (lawyers, doctors, engineers, teachers) and clerks. They grew in number and wealth with industrialisation and commerce, and believed in individual effort, property, education, thrift and respectability. They supported liberalism - constitutional government, freedom of the press and speech, free trade (Adam Smith's 'The Wealth of Nations', 1776) and limited government.

In Britain, middle-class pressure led to the Reform Act of 1832, which extended voting rights to middle-class men, and the repeal of the Corn Laws (1846). In France, they led the revolutions of 1830 and 1848; in Germany, they supported national unification. They also promoted social reforms, education and the ideal of a domestic family life ('Victorian values'). Marxists saw the bourgeoisie as the ruling class of capitalism opposed to the proletariat.
section-149: Britain consolidated its rule in India (Crown rule from 1858), conquered Burma (1885), Malaya and Singapore, and fought the Opium Wars (1839-1842, 1856-1860) with China, gaining Hong Kong and opening treaty ports. France conquered Indochina (Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos) from 1858 to 1893. The Dutch extended control over Indonesia. Russia expanded into Central Asia and the Far East. The USA took the Philippines (1898). Japan, after the Meiji Restoration (1868), became an imperialist power, defeating China (1894-1895, gaining Taiwan) and Russia (1904-1905), and annexing Korea (1910).

China was divided into 'spheres of influence' by European powers and Japan; the USA proposed the 'Open Door Policy' (1899). Only Japan and Siam (Thailand) avoided colonisation. Motives for imperialism included economic interests (markets, raw materials, investment - J. A. Hobson and Lenin's 'Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism', 1916), strategic rivalry, nationalism, Social Darwinism and the 'civilising mission' ('the white man's burden', Rudyard Kipling).
section-150: In 1870, Europeans controlled only about 10 percent of Africa, mostly coastal areas; by 1914, they controlled about 90 percent. The Berlin Conference (1884-1885), called by Bismarck, laid down rules for partition: a European power had to effectively occupy territory to claim it. King Leopold II of Belgium got the Congo Free State as his personal property, where terrible atrocities were committed in the rubber trade.

Britain ('Cape to Cairo', Cecil Rhodes) took Egypt (1882), Sudan, Nigeria, the Gold Coast, Kenya, Uganda, Rhodesia and South Africa (after the Boer War, 1899-1902); France took most of West and North Africa (Algeria, Tunisia, Morocco, Senegal, French Sudan) and Madagascar; Germany took Togo, Cameroon, South-West Africa (Namibia, where the Herero and Nama genocide took place, 1904-1908) and Tanganyika; Italy took Libya, Eritrea and Somalia; Portugal kept Angola and Mozambique. Only Ethiopia (which defeated Italy at Adwa, 1896) and Liberia remained independent. Resistance included the Ashanti, Zulu (Isandlwana, 1879), Maji Maji (1905-1907) and Mahdist Sudan. Artificial borders drawn in Europe caused later conflicts.
section-151: US President James Monroe announced the doctrine in his message to Congress on 2 December 1823, largely written by Secretary of State John Quincy Adams. It declared that the Americas were no longer open to European colonisation; that any European intervention in the independent states of the Western Hemisphere would be considered a threat to the USA; and that the USA would not interfere in European affairs or existing European colonies.

It was a response to fears that European powers (the Holy Alliance) would help Spain recover its Latin American colonies, which had become independent (1810-1825), and to Russian claims on the Pacific coast. Britain, interested in Latin American trade, supported it with its navy. The Roosevelt Corollary (1904) of Theodore Roosevelt claimed a US right to intervene in Latin American countries to maintain order ('big stick' policy). The doctrine became the basis of US dominance in the Western Hemisphere.
section-152: Causes: the Cuban struggle for independence from Spain (1895), Spanish brutality (General Weyler's reconcentration camps), sensational 'yellow journalism' by newspapers of William Randolph Hearst and Joseph Pulitzer, American economic interests in Cuban sugar and the mysterious explosion of the battleship USS Maine in Havana harbour (February 1898), which killed 266 sailors ('Remember the Maine!').

The war (April-August 1898) was short: Commodore George Dewey destroyed the Spanish fleet at Manila Bay; Theodore Roosevelt's 'Rough Riders' fought at San Juan Hill in Cuba. By the Treaty of Paris (December 1898), Spain gave Cuba independence (under US influence - the Platt Amendment, 1901, allowed US intervention and the base at Guantanamo Bay), and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to the USA for 20 million dollars. Hawaii was annexed separately (1898). The Philippine-American War (1899-1902) followed. The war made the USA a world power with overseas colonies.
section-153: Long-term causes (often remembered as MAIN): Militarism - an arms race, especially the Anglo-German naval race (Dreadnought battleships) and military plans like Germany's Schlieffen Plan; Alliances - the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy, 1882) and the Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain, formed by the Franco-Russian Alliance 1894, Entente Cordiale 1904 and Anglo-Russian Entente 1907); Imperialism - colonial rivalries, the Moroccan crises (1905, 1911); and Nationalism - French desire for revenge over Alsace-Lorraine, Pan-Slavism, Serbian nationalism and German ambitions (Weltpolitik under Kaiser William II).

The Balkans were the 'powder keg of Europe': Austria-Hungary's annexation of Bosnia (1908) angered Serbia; the Balkan Wars (1912-1913) increased tensions. The immediate cause was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb of the Black Hand society. Austria-Hungary, backed by Germany's 'blank cheque', issued an ultimatum to Serbia and declared war on 28 July 1914; Russia mobilised; Germany declared war on Russia and France and invaded Belgium, bringing Britain in (4 August 1914). The Fischer thesis (1961) emphasised Germany's responsibility.
section-154: The Paris Peace Conference (1919) was dominated by the 'Big Four': Woodrow Wilson (USA), David Lloyd George (Britain), Georges Clemenceau (France) and Vittorio Orlando (Italy). Wilson's Fourteen Points (January 1918) called for open diplomacy, free trade, disarmament, self-determination and a League of Nations. The Treaty of Versailles (28 June 1919) with Germany included the 'war guilt' clause (Article 231), heavy reparations (fixed at 132 billion gold marks in 1921), loss of Alsace-Lorraine to France, the Polish Corridor, the Saar under League control, loss of all colonies, demilitarisation of the Rhineland and limits on the army (100,000 men) and navy. Other treaties: St Germain (Austria), Trianon (Hungary), Neuilly (Bulgaria) and Sèvres (Turkey, revised at Lausanne, 1923). New states emerged: Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, the Baltic states.

The League of Nations (founded 1920, headquarters Geneva) aimed at collective security, disarmament and settling disputes. It had an Assembly, Council, Secretariat, the Permanent Court of International Justice and agencies such as the International Labour Organization (ILO). It settled some minor disputes (the Aaland Islands, 1921) and did valuable humanitarian work. Weaknesses: the USA never joined (the Senate rejected the treaty); Germany and the USSR were excluded at first; decisions required unanimity; it had no army; and Britain and France were reluctant. It failed to stop Japan in Manchuria (1931), Italy in Ethiopia (1935-1936) and German aggression, and collapsed with the Second World War. It was replaced by the UN in 1945-1946.
section-155: Causes: Tsarist autocracy under Nicholas II; poverty of peasants (serfdom was abolished only in 1861) and workers; the defeat by Japan (1904-1905) and the 1905 Revolution (Bloody Sunday), which led to the Duma (parliament) with limited powers; the influence of Rasputin at court; and especially the heavy losses, food shortages and economic collapse caused by the First World War. Marxist parties included the Social Democrats, split into Bolsheviks (Lenin) and Mensheviks (1903).

The February Revolution (March 1917, Western calendar): strikes and bread riots in Petrograd, joined by soldiers, forced Nicholas II to abdicate. A Provisional Government (Prince Lvov, then Alexander Kerensky) shared power with the Petrograd Soviet ('dual power'), but continued the war. Lenin returned (April Theses: 'Peace, Land, Bread' and 'All power to the Soviets'). In the October Revolution (7 November 1917), the Bolsheviks, led by Lenin and Trotsky, seized power. They withdrew from the war (Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, March 1918), nationalised land and industry, and won the Civil War (1918-1921) against the 'Whites' and foreign intervention. The USSR was formed in 1922. Lenin's New Economic Policy (1921) allowed some private trade; after his death (1924), Stalin introduced Five-Year Plans and collectivisation.
section-156: Benito Mussolini, a former socialist, founded the Fascist movement (Fasci di Combattimento) in 1919. Italy was discontented after the war ('mutilated victory' - it did not gain the territories it expected), and suffered unemployment, inflation, strikes and fear of communism. Fascist squads (Blackshirts) attacked socialists. After the 'March on Rome' (October 1922), King Victor Emmanuel III appointed Mussolini Prime Minister. After the murder of the socialist Giacomo Matteotti (1924), Mussolini established a dictatorship (1925-1926), calling himself Il Duce.

Features of fascism: extreme nationalism; a one-party totalitarian state ('Everything within the state, nothing outside the state'); the cult of the leader; rejection of liberal democracy, socialism and class struggle; the corporate state (organising employers and workers in corporations under state control); glorification of war and violence; propaganda and youth organisations. Mussolini signed the Lateran Treaty (1929) with the Pope, invaded Ethiopia (1935-1936), formed the Rome-Berlin Axis (1936) and joined the Second World War. He was overthrown in 1943 and killed by partisans in 1945.
section-157: Adolf Hitler, an Austrian-born veteran, led the National Socialist German Workers' Party (NSDAP). After the failed Munich Beer Hall Putsch (1923), he wrote 'Mein Kampf' in prison, setting out his ideas: the superiority of the 'Aryan' race, antisemitism, Lebensraum (living space) in the East, hatred of communism and the Treaty of Versailles. Germany's Weimar Republic (1919-1933) faced reparations, hyperinflation (1923), political violence and especially the Great Depression, which caused mass unemployment (6 million by 1932). The Nazis became the largest party in the Reichstag (July 1932), and Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933.

After the Reichstag fire (February 1933), the Enabling Act (March 1933) gave him dictatorial powers. He banned other parties and trade unions, purged rivals (the Night of the Long Knives, 1934), became Führer after Hindenburg's death (1934), and used the Gestapo, SS and propaganda (Goebbels). Jews were persecuted - the Nuremberg Laws (1935) removed their citizenship; Kristallnacht (November 1938); and in the Second World War, the Holocaust killed about six million Jews, along with Roma, disabled people and others, in concentration and extermination camps such as Auschwitz. Hitler rearmed Germany, remilitarised the Rhineland (1936), annexed Austria (Anschluss, 1938) and the Sudetenland (Munich Agreement, 1938), and invaded Poland (1939).
section-158: The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 ('Black Tuesday', 29 October) in New York began the Great Depression. Causes included overproduction in agriculture and industry, unequal distribution of income, speculation and buying shares on credit, weak banks, high tariffs (the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, 1930) and the dependence of Europe on American loans (the Dawes and Young Plans).

Effects: banks failed, industrial production fell by nearly half in the USA, world trade fell by about two-thirds, and unemployment reached 25 percent in the USA and 30 percent in Germany. In India, prices of agricultural products fell sharply, hurting peasants and contributing to the Civil Disobedience movement. Responses: Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal (1933), with public works, social security and bank regulation; John Maynard Keynes' theory of government spending; protectionism; and in some countries, the rise of dictatorships (Hitler) and militarism (Japan). The Depression discredited liberal capitalism for many and contributed to the Second World War.
section-159: Causes: the harsh Treaty of Versailles and German resentment; the failure of the League of Nations; the Great Depression; the rise of fascism and Nazism; Japanese militarism (invasion of Manchuria, 1931; war with China from 1937); the policy of appeasement by Britain (Neville Chamberlain) and France (the Munich Agreement, 1938); the Rome-Berlin-Tokyo Axis; and the Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact (August 1939). Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939; Britain and France declared war on 3 September.

Course: German Blitzkrieg conquered Poland, Denmark, Norway, the Netherlands, Belgium and France (1940); Britain survived the Battle of Britain (1940); Germany invaded the USSR (Operation Barbarossa, June 1941); Japan attacked Pearl Harbor (7 December 1941), bringing the USA into the war. Turning points: Midway (1942), El Alamein (1942) and Stalingrad (1942-1943). The Allies landed in Normandy (D-Day, 6 June 1944). Germany surrendered on 8 May 1945 (VE Day) after Hitler's suicide. After atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan surrendered (15 August, formally 2 September 1945). About 70-85 million people died. Results: the defeat of fascism, the rise of the USA and USSR as superpowers, the Cold War, the division of Germany, decolonisation and the founding of the UN.
section-160: In 1938, German scientists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann discovered nuclear fission; Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained it. Fearing that Nazi Germany would build an atomic bomb, physicists Leo Szilard and Albert Einstein wrote a letter to President Roosevelt (August 1939). The Manhattan Project (1942-1946), led by General Leslie Groves with J. Robert Oppenheimer as scientific director at Los Alamos, New Mexico, employed over 100,000 people, with British and Canadian participation.

The first atomic bomb test, 'Trinity', took place on 16 July 1945 in New Mexico. The USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima ('Little Boy', uranium, 6 August 1945) and Nagasaki ('Fat Man', plutonium, 9 August 1945), killing about 200,000 people by the end of 1945, many from radiation. Historians debate whether the bombing was necessary to end the war, or partly intended to intimidate the USSR. The USSR tested its first bomb in 1949, beginning the nuclear arms race of the Cold War.
section-161: The Atlantic Charter (1941) of Roosevelt and Churchill and the Declaration by United Nations (1942) prepared the way. The Dumbarton Oaks Conference (1944) drafted proposals; the Yalta Conference (1945) agreed on voting arrangements; and the UN Charter was signed by 50 countries at the San Francisco Conference on 26 June 1945. The UN came into existence on 24 October 1945 (UN Day), with its headquarters in New York. India was a founding member.

Main organs: the General Assembly (all members, one vote each); the Security Council (five permanent members with veto power - the USA, USSR/Russia, Britain, France and China - and ten non-permanent members), responsible for international peace and security; the Economic and Social Council; the Trusteeship Council (now inactive); the International Court of Justice (The Hague); and the Secretariat headed by the Secretary-General. Specialised agencies include UNESCO, WHO, FAO, UNICEF, ILO, IMF and the World Bank. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) was adopted. The UN has conducted peacekeeping missions (India has been a major contributor), supported decolonisation and development, but has been criticised for the veto and Cold War paralysis.
section-163: Napoleon: rose through Revolutionary wars; became First Consul (1799) and Emperor (1804); introduced the Civil Code, Concordat, centralised administration and education; conquered much of Europe (Austerlitz, Jena, Wagram), reorganised Germany and Italy and spread revolutionary principles; failed with the Continental System, Spain and Russia (1812); defeated at Leipzig (1813) and Waterloo (1815). Congress of Vienna (1814-1815): Metternich, Castlereagh, Alexander I, Hardenberg and Talleyrand restored legitimate monarchs, created a balance of power and buffer states, and established the Concert of Europe. It brought peace among great powers but suppressed liberalism and nationalism, leading to revolutions in 1820-1821, 1830 and 1848.

Italian unification: the Risorgimento - Mazzini (the soul, Young Italy), Cavour (the brain, diplomacy and alliance with France), Garibaldi (the sword, the Thousand) and Victor Emmanuel II; wars of 1859 and 1866; Kingdom of Italy proclaimed 1861; Rome captured 1870. German unification: the Zollverein, the failure of 1848, Bismarck's 'blood and iron', three wars (Denmark 1864, Austria 1866, France 1870-1871) and the proclamation of the German Empire at Versailles (1871).

Effects: the emergence of two new great powers changed the balance of power; Germany became the dominant continental power, leading to French hostility over Alsace-Lorraine and the formation of alliances that contributed to the First World War. Nationalism, initially liberal, increasingly became conservative and aggressive in the late nineteenth century.
section-164: Industrial Revolution: began in Britain (c. 1760) due to coal, iron, capital, colonies, agricultural changes and inventions (textile machines, steam engine, railways); spread to Europe, the USA and Japan; a Second Industrial Revolution (steel, electricity, chemicals, oil, automobiles) followed. Social effects: urbanisation, factory labour, poor working and living conditions, child labour, the rise of the working class and trade unions, socialism (Marx), and reforms (Factory Acts, extension of the vote). The middle classes grew powerful, promoting liberalism, free trade, education and parliamentary reform (Reform Act 1832).

Imperialism: motivated by the need for raw materials, markets and investment (Hobson, Lenin), strategic rivalry, nationalism, missionary zeal and Social Darwinism. In Asia: British India and Burma, French Indochina, Dutch Indonesia, the Opium Wars and spheres of influence in China, Japanese imperialism (Taiwan, Korea) and the US annexation of the Philippines. In Africa: the Scramble for Africa after the Berlin Conference (1884-1885), leaving only Ethiopia and Liberia independent, with brutal exploitation (the Congo) and resistance movements.

Americas: the Monroe Doctrine (1823) opposed new European colonisation, and the Roosevelt Corollary (1904) asserted US police power. The Spanish-American War (1898) made the USA a colonial power (Puerto Rico, Guam, the Philippines, influence over Cuba). Imperialism led to rivalries that contributed to the First World War and later to anti-colonial nationalism.
section-165: First World War (1914-1918): long-term causes - militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism (MAIN) and the Balkan crisis; immediate cause - the Sarajevo assassination (28 June 1914). Course: the Western Front (trench warfare - the Marne, Verdun, the Somme), the Eastern Front, Gallipoli, the war at sea (U-boats, the sinking of the Lusitania), US entry (1917) and the Armistice (11 November 1918). About 9-10 million soldiers died. New weapons included machine guns, poison gas, tanks and aircraft.

Peace and League: the Paris Peace Conference and the Treaty of Versailles (war guilt, reparations, territorial losses, disarmament) created resentment in Germany; new states emerged on the principle of self-determination; the League of Nations was created but was weak (no US, unanimity, no army) and failed in Manchuria and Ethiopia. Russian Revolutions (1917): the February Revolution ended Tsarism; the October Revolution brought the Bolsheviks to power under Lenin; the Civil War, War Communism, NEP and Stalin's Five-Year Plans and collectivisation followed, creating the world's first communist state.

Interwar turmoil: fascism in Italy (Mussolini, 1922) and Nazism in Germany (Hitler, 1933) arose from postwar discontent, economic crisis, fear of communism and weak democracies. The Great Depression (from 1929) caused mass unemployment and political extremism; responses included the New Deal and Keynesian ideas. Militarist Japan, aggressive Italy and Germany, and the policy of appeasement set the stage for the Second World War.
section-166: Causes: the Treaty of Versailles, the failure of the League, the Great Depression, fascist and Nazi expansionism, Japanese militarism, appeasement (Munich, 1938) and the Nazi-Soviet Pact (1939). The war began with Germany's invasion of Poland (1 September 1939). Phases: Axis victories (1939-1942) in Europe, North Africa and Asia; turning points (Midway, El Alamein, Stalingrad, 1942-1943); and Allied victories (1943-1945), including the D-Day landings (1944), the Soviet advance to Berlin and the Pacific island-hopping campaign. The Holocaust killed six million Jews.

The atomic bomb: nuclear fission (1938), the Einstein-Szilard letter (1939), the Manhattan Project (Oppenheimer, Los Alamos), the Trinity test (July 1945) and the bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki (August 1945), leading to Japan's surrender. Consequences: the USA and USSR emerged as superpowers; Europe was devastated and divided; Germany and Korea were divided; colonial empires were weakened, leading to decolonisation (including India's independence in 1947); the nuclear age and arms race began; the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials prosecuted war crimes.

The United Nations (1945): established by the San Francisco Charter to maintain peace, promote cooperation and human rights; its organs include the General Assembly, the Security Council (with veto powers of five permanent members), ECOSOC, the International Court of Justice and the Secretariat, along with specialised agencies. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) set global standards. Compared with the League, the UN has wider membership and peacekeeping forces, though the veto has often paralysed it.
section-169: Origins: ideological conflict between capitalism and communism, wartime disagreements (the Yalta and Potsdam conferences, 1945), Soviet control of Eastern Europe (Churchill's 'Iron Curtain' speech at Fulton, 1946), and the US policy of containment (George Kennan). The Truman Doctrine (1947) offered support to countries resisting communism (Greece and Turkey); the Marshall Plan (1947-1951) provided about 13 billion dollars to rebuild Western Europe; the USSR responded with Cominform (1947) and Comecon (1949).

The Berlin Blockade (1948-1949) and Berlin Airlift; the division of Germany into the Federal Republic (West) and the German Democratic Republic (East) in 1949; NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955); the Soviet atomic bomb (1949); the Korean War (1950-1953); the Hungarian uprising crushed by the USSR (1956); the arms and space race (Sputnik, 1957); and the construction of the Berlin Wall (August 1961). Khrushchev proposed 'peaceful coexistence' after Stalin's death (1953), but tensions continued.
section-170: After Fidel Castro's revolution in Cuba (1959) and the failed US-backed Bay of Pigs invasion (April 1961), Khrushchev secretly placed nuclear missiles in Cuba, partly to protect Cuba and to balance US missiles in Turkey and Italy. On 14 October 1962, US U-2 spy planes photographed the missile sites. President John F. Kennedy announced a naval 'quarantine' (blockade) of Cuba on 22 October.

For thirteen days the world was close to nuclear war. On 28 October, Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles in exchange for a US promise not to invade Cuba, and secretly the USA agreed to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey. Results: a Moscow-Washington 'hotline' (1963), the Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963), and a realisation of the dangers of nuclear confrontation, contributing to détente.
section-171: Détente (French for 'relaxation') refers to the easing of tensions from the late 1960s to the late 1970s, under US President Richard Nixon and National Security Adviser Henry Kissinger and Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev. Factors: the dangers shown by the Cuban crisis, the cost of the arms race, the Sino-Soviet split, the US involvement in Vietnam, and West German Chancellor Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik (normalising relations with Eastern Europe).

Achievements: the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968); Nixon's visit to China (1972); the Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty (SALT I) and the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty (1972); the Apollo-Soyuz joint space mission (1975); and the Helsinki Accords (1975), which recognised Europe's borders and committed signatories to human rights. Détente ended with the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (December 1979), the US boycott of the Moscow Olympics (1980) and Ronald Reagan's arms build-up ('Second Cold War'), until Gorbachev's reforms led to the end of the Cold War (1989-1991).
section-172: Western Europe: the Marshall Plan, the Bretton Woods system (IMF and World Bank, 1944), Keynesian economic policies, the welfare state (Britain's National Health Service, 1948) and European integration - the European Coal and Steel Community (1951) and the European Economic Community (Treaty of Rome, 1957) - led to rapid growth in the 1950s and 1960s, called the 'economic miracle' (Wirtschaftswunder) in West Germany, the 'Trente Glorieuses' in France and the 'economic boom' in Italy.

Eastern Europe: under Soviet control, countries adopted Soviet-style planned economies, collectivised agriculture and nationalised industry, coordinated through Comecon. They achieved industrial growth and full employment, but with lower living standards, shortages of consumer goods and political repression, leading to uprisings in East Germany (1953), Hungary (1956), Czechoslovakia (the Prague Spring, 1968) and Poland (Solidarity, 1980-1981). The contrast between East and West contributed to the eventual collapse of communism in 1989.
section-173: Factors: the weakening of European powers in the Second World War; the growth of nationalist movements; the Atlantic Charter's principle of self-determination; the opposition of the USA and USSR to colonialism; and the UN. Asia: India and Pakistan (1947), Burma and Ceylon (1948), Indonesia (1949, after war with the Dutch), Indochina (after the French defeat at Dien Bien Phu, 1954), Malaya (1957). Africa: Ghana under Kwame Nkrumah (1957) was the first sub-Saharan country to become independent; 1960 was the 'Year of Africa', with 17 countries gaining independence; Algeria won independence after a brutal war with France (1954-1962); Kenya after the Mau Mau uprising (1963); Portuguese colonies after the 1974 revolution in Portugal; Zimbabwe (1980) and Namibia (1990).

Decolonisation was peaceful in some cases and violent in others. New nations faced problems of poverty, artificial borders, ethnic conflict, military coups and neo-colonialism (continued economic dependence on former colonial powers). The UN's Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples (1960) supported the process.
section-174: After the 1911 Revolution, China was divided among warlords. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP, founded 1921) and the Kuomintang (KMT) cooperated in the First United Front (1923-1927), but Chiang Kai-shek turned on the communists in the Shanghai massacre (1927). The communists, led by Mao Zedong, built rural bases (the Jiangxi Soviet), and escaped encirclement through the Long March (1934-1935) to Yan'an. During the war with Japan (1937-1945), the Second United Front formed, and the communists expanded their support among peasants through guerrilla warfare and land reform.

In the civil war (1946-1949), the communists defeated the KMT, which was weakened by corruption, inflation and loss of popular support. Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949 at Tiananmen Square in Beijing; Chiang fled to Taiwan. The revolution created the world's most populous communist state, signed the Sino-Soviet Treaty (1950) and changed the balance of power in Asia, leading to US involvement in Korea and support for Taiwan.
section-175: Korea, a Japanese colony since 1910, was divided at the 38th parallel in 1945, with Soviet troops in the north and US troops in the south. In 1948, the Republic of Korea (South, under Syngman Rhee) and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North, under Kim Il-sung) were established. On 25 June 1950, North Korea invaded the South with Soviet and Chinese approval.

The UN Security Council (with the USSR absent in protest over China's seat) authorised a UN force, mostly American, under General Douglas MacArthur. After the Inchon landing (September 1950), UN forces pushed north towards the Yalu River, provoking Chinese intervention with hundreds of thousands of 'volunteers' (October 1950). The war became a stalemate near the 38th parallel. MacArthur was dismissed by Truman (1951) for wanting to attack China. An armistice was signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953; no peace treaty has been signed, and Korea remains divided by the Demilitarised Zone. About 3 million people died. India played a role through the Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission chaired by General K. S. Thimayya.
section-176: First Indochina War (1946-1954): Ho Chi Minh's Viet Minh declared Vietnam's independence (September 1945) and fought France. The French defeat at Dien Bien Phu (May 1954) led to the Geneva Accords (1954), which divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel, with elections planned for 1956 that never took place. North Vietnam was communist; South Vietnam was led by Ngo Dinh Diem with US support.

Second Indochina (Vietnam) War (c. 1955-1975): the communist Viet Cong (National Liberation Front) fought in the South with Northern support. The USA increased involvement based on the 'domino theory'; after the Gulf of Tonkin incident (1964), President Lyndon Johnson sent over 500,000 troops and bombed the North (Operation Rolling Thunder). The Tet Offensive (1968) turned US public opinion against the war; the anti-war movement grew. Nixon's 'Vietnamisation' reduced US troops, and the Paris Peace Accords (1973) ended US involvement. North Vietnamese forces captured Saigon on 30 April 1975, uniting Vietnam. About 2-3 million Vietnamese died. Wars also affected Cambodia (Khmer Rouge genocide, 1975-1979) and Laos.
section-177: Background: Zionism (Theodor Herzl, 1896) sought a Jewish homeland in Palestine; the Balfour Declaration (1917) by Britain supported a 'national home for the Jewish people'; Britain ruled Palestine under a League of Nations mandate, and Jewish immigration increased, especially after the Holocaust, causing conflict with Arabs. The UN Partition Plan (1947) proposed separate Jewish and Arab states. Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948; the first Arab-Israeli war followed, and about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled (the Nakba).

Later wars: the Suez Crisis (1956), when Israel, Britain and France attacked Egypt after Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal; the Six-Day War (1967), when Israel captured the West Bank, East Jerusalem, Gaza, the Sinai and the Golan Heights; the Yom Kippur War (1973) and the Arab oil embargo. The Camp David Accords (1978) led to the Egypt-Israel peace treaty (1979). The Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO, 1964, led by Yasser Arafat) and the intifadas (1987, 2000) continued the struggle; the Oslo Accords (1993) created the Palestinian Authority, but a final settlement has not been achieved. The conflict has continued into the 2020s, including the war in Gaza following the attacks of 7 October 2023.
section-178: Pan-Africanism, promoted by W. E. B. Du Bois, Marcus Garvey, Kwame Nkrumah and the Pan-African Congresses (Manchester, 1945), inspired the independence movements. The Organisation of African Unity (OAU, 1963) was founded at Addis Ababa to promote unity and end colonialism; it became the African Union (2002). New leaders included Nkrumah (Ghana), Jomo Kenyatta (Kenya), Julius Nyerere (Tanzania, 'ujamaa' socialism), Patrice Lumumba (Congo, assassinated 1961), Léopold Senghor (Senegal) and Gamal Abdel Nasser (Egypt).

Challenges: artificial colonial borders and ethnic divisions (the Nigerian Civil War / Biafra, 1967-1970); military coups and one-party states; Cold War interventions (the Congo crisis, Angola, Ethiopia); dependence on exports of raw materials; debt crises and structural adjustment programmes of the 1980s; famines (Ethiopia, 1984-1985); and the Rwandan genocide (1994). Since the 1990s, many African countries have moved towards multiparty democracy and economic growth.
section-179: Apartheid ('separateness') was a system of institutionalised racial segregation introduced by the National Party government in 1948 under D. F. Malan. Laws included the Population Registration Act (1950), classifying people by race; the Group Areas Act (1950), segregating residential areas; the Bantu Education Act (1953); pass laws restricting black Africans' movement; and the creation of 'Bantustans' (homelands). Opposition came from the African National Congress (ANC, 1912). The Sharpeville massacre (1960), when police killed 69 protesters, led to the banning of the ANC; Nelson Mandela was imprisoned in 1964 (Rivonia Trial) on Robben Island. The Soweto uprising (1976) and Steve Biko's death in custody (1977) intensified resistance.

International pressure included UN sanctions, sports boycotts and economic disinvestment; India was the first country to impose trade sanctions on South Africa (1946). President F. W. de Klerk lifted the ban on the ANC and released Mandela in February 1990. Negotiations led to the first multiracial elections in April 1994, and Mandela became President. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, 1996) investigated human rights abuses. Mandela and de Klerk shared the Nobel Peace Prize (1993).
section-180: The Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) was founded at the Belgrade Conference (1961) by Jawaharlal Nehru (India), Josip Broz Tito (Yugoslavia), Gamal Abdel Nasser (Egypt), Sukarno (Indonesia) and Kwame Nkrumah (Ghana), building on the Bandung Asian-African Conference (1955) and its 'Ten Principles'. It drew on India's Panchsheel principles (1954) of peaceful coexistence, signed with China.

Aims: to stay independent of the US and Soviet blocs; oppose colonialism, racism and apartheid; support disarmament and world peace; and promote economic development and a New International Economic Order (NIEO, 1974). NAM grew to about 120 members, the largest grouping of states after the UN. Critics noted that some members were aligned in practice (India signed a treaty with the USSR in 1971) and that NAM lost relevance after the Cold War, though it continues to meet.
section-181: The Group of 77 (G77) was formed on 15 June 1964 by 77 developing countries at the end of the first United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) in Geneva. Its 'Joint Declaration' called for a fairer world economic system. It now has over 130 members (with China often associated as 'G77 and China') but keeps its original name.

It promotes the collective economic interests of developing countries in the UN, demanding fairer terms of trade, stable prices for primary commodities, access to markets of developed countries, technology transfer, debt relief and development aid. It pushed for the NIEO declaration (1974) and South-South cooperation. In climate negotiations, the G77 and China argue for 'common but differentiated responsibilities'. Its effectiveness has been limited by divisions among its diverse members.
section-182: Japan: after defeat in 1945, the US occupation under General MacArthur introduced a democratic constitution (1947), which renounced war (Article 9), land reform and the break-up of zaibatsu (business conglomerates). The Korean War boosted Japan's economy. With high savings and investment, government guidance (MITI), lifetime employment, technology adoption and exports (cars, electronics - Toyota, Sony), Japan achieved rapid growth (around 10 percent a year in the 1960s) and became the world's second-largest economy by 1968. The bursting of an asset bubble in 1990-1991 led to the 'lost decade'.

South Korea under Park Chung-hee (1961-1979) and Taiwan under the KMT followed export-oriented industrialisation with strong state guidance, land reform, education and US aid, becoming 'newly industrialised economies' (the 'Four Asian Tigers' with Hong Kong and Singapore). South Korea developed chaebols (Samsung, Hyundai). Both democratised in the late 1980s. Explanations of the 'East Asian miracle' include the developmental state, Confucian values, education, high savings and favourable Cold War conditions.
section-183: China and the USSR signed the Treaty of Friendship (1950), and the USSR provided aid and technology. Relations deteriorated after Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin (1956) and his policy of 'peaceful coexistence' with the West, which Mao criticised as 'revisionism'. Mao's Great Leap Forward rejected the Soviet development model. The USSR withdrew its technical advisers (1960) and refused to help China build nuclear weapons; China tested its own atomic bomb in 1964.

Other disputes included the Soviet neutrality in the Sino-Indian War (1962), competition for leadership of the communist world and the Third World, and border clashes along the Ussuri River (Zhenbao Island, 1969). The split led China to improve relations with the USA - 'ping-pong diplomacy', Kissinger's secret visit (1971), China's admission to the UN in place of Taiwan (1971) and Nixon's visit (1972). Relations normalised only in 1989 under Gorbachev.
section-184: Kim Il-sung (ruled 1948-1994) created a communist state with a personality cult. He developed the ideology of Juche (self-reliance), emphasising independence in politics, economy and defence, and later Songun ('military first' policy, under Kim Jong-il). Power passed dynastically to his son Kim Jong-il (1994-2011) and grandson Kim Jong-un (from 2011), making North Korea a hereditary communist state.

North Korea has a centrally planned economy and is one of the most isolated countries in the world. After the collapse of the USSR, it suffered a severe famine in the 1990s ('the Arduous March'), killing hundreds of thousands. It withdrew from the Non-Proliferation Treaty (2003) and conducted nuclear tests from 2006 and missile tests, leading to UN sanctions. Summits between Kim Jong-un and South Korea's Moon Jae-in and US President Donald Trump (2018-2019) did not produce lasting agreements.
section-185: Guatemala: President Jacobo Árbenz carried out land reform that affected the US-owned United Fruit Company; the CIA organised a coup that overthrew him (1954). Cuba: Fidel Castro and Che Guevara overthrew the dictator Fulgencio Batista (1959); Castro nationalised US property and allied with the USSR; the USA imposed an embargo, sponsored the failed Bay of Pigs invasion (1961) and faced the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962). The 'Alliance for Progress' (1961) of Kennedy offered economic aid to counter revolution.

Chile: the socialist President Salvador Allende, elected in 1970, nationalised copper mines; with US support, General Augusto Pinochet overthrew him in a coup on 11 September 1973, and ruled as dictator until 1990, with widespread human rights abuses and free-market reforms. Nicaragua: the Sandinistas overthrew the Somoza dictatorship (1979); the Reagan administration funded the 'Contra' rebels, leading to the Iran-Contra affair (1986). These cases show how Cold War fears of communism led the USA to support dictatorships and interventions, while Latin American struggles were rooted in inequality, land, foreign economic domination and nationalism.
section-187: Origins and first Cold War (1945-1961): ideological rivalry, the Soviet takeover of Eastern Europe, the Iron Curtain, containment, the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan, the Berlin Blockade and Airlift, NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955), the nuclear and space race, the Korean War and the Berlin Wall (1961). Historians debate responsibility: orthodox (Soviet expansionism), revisionist (US economic imperialism) and post-revisionist (mutual misperception) schools.

Crisis and détente: the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) brought the world close to nuclear war and led to the hotline and the Test Ban Treaty (1963). Détente (late 1960s-1970s) included the NPT (1968), SALT I and the ABM Treaty (1972), Ostpolitik and the Helsinki Accords (1975). It collapsed with the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (1979). The Cold War ended after Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika, the fall of the Berlin Wall (1989), German reunification (1990) and the dissolution of the USSR (December 1991).

Economic recovery: Western Europe recovered quickly with Marshall aid, the welfare state and European integration (ECSC 1951, EEC 1957), achieving an 'economic miracle'; Eastern Europe developed planned economies under Comecon with industrial growth but shortages and repression. Economic competition became part of the Cold War, and the West's economic success contributed to its eventual victory.
section-188: Asia: India's independence (1947) inspired others; decolonisation followed in Burma, Ceylon, Indonesia (Sukarno), Malaya, and Indochina. Southeast Asian nationalism included the struggles of Ho Chi Minh, Sukarno and Aung San. The Chinese Revolution (1949) created a communist state; the Korean War (1950-1953) left Korea divided; the Vietnam Wars (1946-1954 and 1955-1975) ended with communist victory and unification. The Arab-Israeli conflict (1948, 1956, 1967, 1973 wars; the Palestinian issue) destabilised West Asia.

Africa: Pan-Africanism and nationalist leaders (Nkrumah, Kenyatta, Nyerere, Lumumba) led to independence for most countries between 1957 and 1975; violent struggles occurred in Algeria, Kenya, Angola, Mozambique and Zimbabwe. The OAU (1963) promoted unity. New states faced artificial borders, ethnic conflict, military coups, one-party rule, Cold War interventions (Congo, Angola), economic dependence, debt and poverty.

End of apartheid: the National Party's apartheid system (from 1948) was resisted by the ANC, Mandela and the black consciousness movement (Biko), with international sanctions. De Klerk's reforms, Mandela's release (1990) and the elections of 1994 ended apartheid, followed by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Decolonisation thus transformed the world from a system of empires into one of nearly 200 sovereign states.
section-189: Non-alignment: newly independent countries did not want to join either Cold War bloc. Nehru's foreign policy of non-alignment, the Panchsheel principles (1954) and the Bandung Conference (1955) led to the founding of the NAM at Belgrade (1961) by Nehru, Tito, Nasser, Sukarno and Nkrumah. NAM opposed colonialism, racism and apartheid, promoted disarmament and peace, and supported the Third World's economic demands. India played a leading role, though its 1971 treaty with the USSR raised questions about its non-alignment.

G77 and the Third World: the G77 (1964), formed at UNCTAD, demanded a New International Economic Order (1974) with fair trade, commodity price stability, technology transfer and aid. The idea of the 'Third World' (coined by Alfred Sauvy in 1952) expressed solidarity among developing countries. However, it became fragmented by different political systems (democracies, military regimes, communist states), economic paths (oil-rich countries after 1973, newly industrialised countries, poor countries), regional conflicts and the end of the Cold War.

East Asia's rise: Japan's postwar recovery to become the second-largest economy; South Korea and Taiwan's export-led industrialisation; and later the rise of China showed that some developing countries could achieve rapid growth through state-guided capitalism, education and exports. This contrasted with the slower growth of many other Third World countries and changed the global economy.
section-190: Sino-Soviet split and China: ideological differences (de-Stalinisation, peaceful coexistence), Mao's rejection of the Soviet model, the withdrawal of Soviet advisers (1960), nuclear disputes and border clashes (1969) broke the alliance. China supported revolutionary movements in Asia and Africa (and built the TAZARA railway in Tanzania-Zambia), competed with the USSR for influence in the Third World and moved closer to the USA (1971-1972). North Korea under Kim Il-sung, Kim Jong-il and Kim Jong-un developed the Juche ideology, a hereditary dictatorship, a militarised economy and nuclear weapons.

Latin America: deep inequality, land concentration and foreign economic domination produced reformist and revolutionary movements. The USA, fearing communism, intervened: the CIA coup in Guatemala (1954), the Bay of Pigs and the embargo against Cuba, support for the Pinochet coup in Chile (1973) and funding of the Contras in Nicaragua (1980s). It also supported military dictatorships in Brazil (1964), Argentina (1976, the 'Dirty War') and elsewhere, through Operation Condor.

Significance: the Cold War was a global conflict fought largely in the developing world through proxy wars, coups and aid, with immense human costs. Local factors - nationalism, social inequality, ethnic and religious divisions - interacted with superpower rivalry. Studying these cases helps explain present-day politics in Asia, Africa and Latin America.
section-193: The Qing (Manchu) dynasty ruled China from 1644. In the nineteenth century, it faced population pressure, corruption, a weak treasury and rebellions. The First Opium War (1839-1842), caused by the British opium trade and Commissioner Lin Zexu's destruction of opium at Canton, ended with the Treaty of Nanking (1842), which ceded Hong Kong to Britain, opened five treaty ports, imposed indemnities and fixed tariffs - the first of the 'unequal treaties'. The Second Opium War (1856-1860) led to further concessions and the burning of the Summer Palace.

The Taiping Rebellion (1850-1864), led by Hong Xiuquan, who claimed to be the brother of Jesus, killed about 20-30 million people. Other rebellions included the Nian and Muslim revolts. The Self-Strengthening Movement (1861-1895) tried to adopt Western technology but was limited. Defeat by Japan (1894-1895) and the 'scramble for concessions' showed Qing weakness. The Hundred Days' Reform (1898) of Emperor Guangxu was crushed by Empress Dowager Cixi.
section-194: The 'Boxers' (Society of Righteous and Harmonious Fists, Yihetuan) arose in Shandong in 1898-1899 among peasants suffering from drought, floods and economic hardship. They practised martial arts and believed they were immune to bullets, and blamed foreigners and Chinese Christians for China's troubles, with the slogan 'Support the Qing, destroy the foreign'.

In 1900, they killed missionaries, Chinese Christians and foreigners, and besieged the foreign legations in Beijing; Empress Dowager Cixi supported them and declared war on the foreign powers. An Eight-Nation Alliance (Britain, France, Germany, Russia, the USA, Japan, Italy and Austria-Hungary) sent about 20,000 troops, captured Beijing and lifted the siege (August 1900).
