The Boxer Protocol (1901) imposed a huge indemnity (450 million taels), allowed foreign troops in Beijing and ordered the execution of officials. The rebellion further weakened the Qing and led to the late Qing reforms (abolition of the civil service examinations in 1905).
section-195: The late Qing reforms (constitutional plans, new army, education) came too late. Revolutionary groups, especially Sun Yat-sen's Tongmenghui (Revolutionary Alliance, 1905), spread anti-Manchu and republican ideas among students, overseas Chinese and soldiers. Anger over the nationalisation of railways (the Railway Protection Movement in Sichuan) and an accidental explosion at Wuchang led to an army mutiny on 10 October 1911 (the Wuchang Uprising, celebrated as 'Double Ten').

Provinces declared independence one after another. Sun Yat-sen returned from abroad and was elected Provisional President of the Republic of China at Nanjing (1 January 1912). To avoid civil war and secure the abdication, Sun agreed that Yuan Shikai, the powerful general of the Beiyang Army, would become president. The last emperor, Puyi (aged six), abdicated on 12 February 1912, ending over 2,000 years of imperial rule.
section-196: Yuan Shikai became president (1912) but became increasingly authoritarian; he suppressed the Kuomintang (KMT, the Nationalist Party formed in 1912), whose leader Song Jiaoren was assassinated (1913), and declared himself emperor (1915-1916), but was forced to abandon the plan and died in 1916. China then fell into the 'warlord era' (1916-1928), when regional military leaders controlled different areas and the Beijing government was weak.

Japan's Twenty-One Demands (1915) and the Versailles Treaty's transfer of German rights in Shandong to Japan provoked the May Fourth Movement (4 May 1919), when students protested in Beijing. It became a broader New Culture Movement, criticising Confucianism and promoting science, democracy, vernacular literature (Lu Xun) and new ideas, including Marxism. This intellectual ferment led to the founding of the CCP (1921) and the reorganisation of the KMT.
section-197: Sun Yat-sen (1866-1925), born in Guangdong and educated in Hawaii and Hong Kong as a doctor, founded the Revive China Society (1894) and later the Tongmenghui (1905). He led several failed uprisings and raised funds among overseas Chinese. He became Provisional President in 1912 but gave the presidency to Yuan Shikai.

Later he established a government in Guangzhou (Canton), reorganised the KMT with Soviet help, formed the First United Front with the CCP (1923-1924) and founded the Whampoa Military Academy (1924), with Chiang Kai-shek as commandant and Zhou Enlai as head of the political department. He died in 1925 while trying to negotiate national unity. Both the KMT and the CCP honour him as the 'Father of the Nation' (Guofu) of modern China.
section-198: Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles of the People (Sanmin Zhuyi), developed from around 1905 and elaborated in lectures in 1924: (1) Minzu - nationalism: freeing China from Manchu rule and foreign imperialism, and achieving unity of China's ethnic groups; (2) Minquan - democracy or people's rights: a republic with elections and a constitution with five branches of government (executive, legislative, judicial, examination and control); and (3) Minsheng - people's livelihood: social welfare, equalisation of land rights (land value tax) and regulation of capital, sometimes described as a form of socialism.

He proposed three stages of revolution: military rule, political tutelage (under the party) and constitutional government. The principles became the official ideology of the KMT and remain influential in Taiwan's constitution.
section-199: In July 1926, the National Revolutionary Army of the KMT, led by Chiang Kai-shek and supported by the CCP and Soviet advisers (Mikhail Borodin), launched the Northern Expedition from Guangzhou to defeat the warlords and unify China. It quickly captured Wuhan, Nanjing and Shanghai, helped by peasant and worker uprisings organised by the communists.

In April 1927, Chiang turned against the communists in the Shanghai Massacre, killing thousands of communists and union workers, ending the First United Front. He established the Nationalist government at Nanjing. The expedition continued and captured Beijing (renamed Beiping) in 1928, and the Manchurian warlord Zhang Xueliang accepted Nationalist authority, formally unifying China under the KMT, although many warlords retained local power.
section-200: Chiang Kai-shek (Jiang Jieshi, 1887-1975) studied military science in Japan, became commandant of the Whampoa Military Academy and, after Sun Yat-sen's death, leader of the KMT. He led the Northern Expedition, broke with the communists (1927), and established the Nanjing government (the 'Nanjing Decade', 1927-1937), which modernised some infrastructure but was authoritarian, corrupt and dependent on landlords and businessmen. He launched 'encirclement campaigns' against the communists and promoted the New Life Movement (1934), based on Confucian values.

In the Xi'an Incident (December 1936), he was kidnapped by Zhang Xueliang and forced to form a Second United Front with the communists against Japan. During the Sino-Japanese War (1937-1945), he moved the capital to Chongqing and received Allied support. After defeat in the Civil War (1949), he retreated to Taiwan, ruled as President of the Republic of China under martial law until his death in 1975, and was succeeded by his son Chiang Ching-kuo.
section-201: The CCP was founded in Shanghai in July 1921 by Chen Duxiu, Li Dazhao and others, including Mao Zedong as a delegate, with help from the Comintern. It initially worked with the KMT (First United Front), organising workers and peasants. After the 1927 massacre, it built rural soviets, especially the Jiangxi Soviet (1931-1934), and the Red Army.

Under Mao's leadership (confirmed at the Zunyi Conference, 1935), the CCP developed a strategy of peasant-based revolution and guerrilla warfare rather than urban uprisings (a departure from orthodox Marxism). From its base at Yan'an, it carried out land reform, rectification campaigns and mass mobilisation. During the war against Japan, its membership grew from about 40,000 (1937) to over 1.2 million (1945). It won the Civil War (1946-1949) and has ruled the People's Republic since 1949.
section-202: Mao Zedong (1893-1976), son of a well-off peasant in Hunan, became a Marxist in Beijing, was a founding member of the CCP and organised peasants (his 'Report on the Peasant Movement in Hunan', 1927). He developed 'Mao Zedong Thought' - adapting Marxism-Leninism to Chinese conditions, with peasants as the main revolutionary force, protracted people's war ('political power grows out of the barrel of a gun'), the mass line and New Democracy.

As Chairman of the CCP and the PRC (from 1949), he led land reform, the campaigns against 'counter-revolutionaries', the first Five-Year Plan (1953-1957), the Hundred Flowers Campaign (1956-1957) and the Anti-Rightist Campaign, the Great Leap Forward (1958-1962) and the Cultural Revolution (1966-1976). His 'Little Red Book' (Quotations from Chairman Mao) became a symbol of the personality cult. He died on 9 September 1976. The CCP's 1981 resolution assessed him as '70 percent right, 30 percent wrong'.
section-203: In October 1934, facing Chiang's fifth encirclement campaign, about 86,000 members of the Red Army broke out of the Jiangxi Soviet. Over the next year they marched about 10,000 kilometres (12,500 km by some counts) through mountains, rivers and marshes across 11 provinces, fighting KMT and warlord forces, and crossing the Dadu River (Luding Bridge) and the Great Snowy Mountains. In January 1935, at the Zunyi Conference, Mao gained leadership of the party.

In October 1935, about 7,000-8,000 survivors reached Shaanxi in the north-west and established a base at Yan'an. Despite enormous losses, the march preserved the communist leadership, spread communist ideas among peasants along the route and became a heroic legend of endurance and commitment. Edgar Snow's 'Red Star Over China' (1937) spread the story internationally.
section-204: Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949. The new government, with Zhou Enlai as Premier, carried out land reform (1950-1953), redistributing land from landlords to peasants (with perhaps one to two million landlords killed), introduced the Marriage Law (1950) giving women equal rights and banning arranged marriages, launched campaigns against corruption and capitalists (Three-Anti and Five-Anti campaigns), and nationalised industry.

China signed the Sino-Soviet Treaty (1950), fought in the Korean War (1950-1953), took control of Tibet (1950-1951), and implemented the First Five-Year Plan (1953-1957) on the Soviet model, emphasising heavy industry. Agriculture was collectivised into cooperatives (1955-1956). The 1954 Constitution established the National People's Congress. Relations with India included Panchsheel (1954), but deteriorated with the Tibetan uprising (1959), the Dalai Lama's flight to India and the 1962 border war.
section-205: Launched in 1958, the Great Leap Forward aimed to rapidly overtake Britain in industrial production within fifteen years by mobilising China's huge labour force. About 700 million peasants were organised into some 26,000 people's communes, with communal kitchens. Backyard furnaces were set up to produce steel, but much of it was useless. Unrealistic targets, false reports of production, the diversion of labour from agriculture, Lysenkoist farming methods, the 'four pests' campaign (killing sparrows, which led to insect plagues) and continued grain exports caused disaster.

The resulting Great Chinese Famine (1959-1961) killed an estimated 15 to 45 million people, the deadliest famine in history. When Defence Minister Peng Dehuai criticised the policy at the Lushan Conference (1959), he was purged. Mao stepped back from day-to-day leadership; Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping introduced pragmatic recovery policies (allowing private plots and markets). The failure contributed to the Sino-Soviet split and later to Mao's attempt to regain power through the Cultural Revolution.
section-206: The Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution (1966-1976) was launched by Mao to restore his authority, purge 'capitalist roaders' and 'revisionists' in the party (such as Liu Shaoqi, who died in prison, and Deng Xiaoping, who was sent to work in a factory), and renew revolutionary spirit. Students formed Red Guards, who attacked teachers, officials and intellectuals, and destroyed the 'Four Olds' (old customs, culture, habits and ideas) - temples, books and historical relics. Schools and universities closed; millions of urban youth were 'sent down' to the countryside.

The Gang of Four, led by Mao's wife Jiang Qing, controlled culture and propaganda. Factional violence led to near civil war, and the army was used to restore order (1967-1969). Lin Biao, Mao's designated successor, died in a plane crash in 1971 after an alleged coup attempt. Hundreds of thousands to perhaps two million people died. After Mao's death (1976), the Gang of Four was arrested. The CCP later called the Cultural Revolution a 'catastrophe' that caused 'the most severe setback and the heaviest losses' since 1949.
section-207: Deng Xiaoping (1904-1997), a veteran of the Long March, was purged twice during the Cultural Revolution, but emerged as China's paramount leader by 1978 (Third Plenum of the Eleventh Central Committee). He promoted the 'Four Modernisations' (agriculture, industry, defence, science and technology) and pragmatic policies ('It does not matter whether a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice').

Reforms: the household responsibility system replaced collective farming; township and village enterprises grew; Special Economic Zones (Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Shantou, Xiamen, 1980) opened to foreign investment; prices were gradually freed; and China joined the world economy. The 'one-child policy' (1979) controlled population growth. Deng called this 'socialism with Chinese characteristics'. Economic growth averaged about 10 percent a year, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty. Politically, he rejected democracy, insisting on the 'Four Cardinal Principles' (socialism, dictatorship of the proletariat, party leadership, Marxism-Leninism-Mao Zedong Thought). His 'Southern Tour' (1992) revived reforms. He negotiated the return of Hong Kong (1997) under 'one country, two systems'.
section-208: In April 1989, after the death of the reformist leader Hu Yaobang, students gathered in Tiananmen Square in Beijing to mourn him and demand political reform, freedom of the press, an end to corruption and dialogue with the government. Workers and citizens joined; protests spread to many cities. Students began a hunger strike in May, during Soviet leader Gorbachev's visit, and erected a 'Goddess of Democracy' statue. General Secretary Zhao Ziyang sympathised with the students but was removed.

The government declared martial law (20 May). On the night of 3-4 June 1989, the People's Liberation Army moved into central Beijing with tanks and troops and fired on protesters; estimates of the dead range from several hundred to several thousand. The image of 'Tank Man' became famous worldwide. Leaders were arrested or fled abroad. Western countries imposed sanctions. The government later strengthened party control, promoted patriotic education and accelerated economic reforms, while the event remains heavily censored in China.
section-209: After Deng, Jiang Zemin (1989-2002) and Hu Jintao (2002-2012) continued economic reform. China joined the World Trade Organization (2001), became the 'workshop of the world' and the largest exporter, and in 2010 overtook Japan to become the world's second-largest economy. It hosted the 2008 Beijing Olympics and the 2010 Shanghai Expo, launched human spaceflight (2003) and expanded investment abroad.

Under Xi Jinping (General Secretary from 2012, President from 2013), China launched the Belt and Road Initiative (2013), a massive infrastructure and investment programme across Asia, Africa and Europe, founded the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (2016), modernised its military, became more assertive in the South China Sea and on its borders (including the clash with India at Galwan in 2020), and increased its role in international organisations. China is now a major global power competing with the USA in trade, technology and strategic influence.
section-210: Achievements: China became the world's largest manufacturer and trading nation, eliminated extreme poverty according to its official standards (2020), built the world's largest high-speed rail network, and became a leader in technologies such as renewable energy, electric vehicles and telecommunications (5G). Under Xi Jinping, the party strengthened its control, removed presidential term limits (2018), promoted 'Xi Jinping Thought' and launched an anti-corruption campaign.

Challenges: income inequality and rural-urban gaps; an ageing population and shrinking workforce (the one-child policy was replaced by a two-child policy in 2016 and a three-child policy in 2021); environmental pollution; a property sector crisis (Evergrande); slowing growth; tensions with the USA (trade war from 2018, technology restrictions) and neighbours; international criticism over human rights in Xinjiang (treatment of Uyghurs), Tibet and Hong Kong (the National Security Law of 2020); and the question of Taiwan. China's future role in the world remains a central issue in global politics.
section-212: Decline of the Qing: internal problems (population pressure, corruption, rebellions - especially the Taiping Rebellion) combined with foreign aggression (Opium Wars and unequal treaties, the loss to Japan in 1894-1895, the scramble for concessions). The Self-Strengthening Movement and the Hundred Days' Reform (1898) failed due to conservative resistance led by Empress Dowager Cixi. The Boxer Rebellion (1899-1901), an anti-foreign peasant movement, was crushed by the Eight-Nation Alliance and led to the humiliating Boxer Protocol.

1911 Revolution: late Qing reforms (abolition of the examination system in 1905, plans for a constitution) came too late; Sun Yat-sen's Tongmenghui spread republican ideas; the Wuchang Uprising (10 October 1911) led to the collapse of the dynasty and the establishment of the Republic (1912), with Sun as Provisional President, followed by Yuan Shikai. Sun's Three Principles - nationalism, democracy and people's livelihood - became the ideology of the KMT.

Republic and warlords: Yuan's dictatorship and failed imperial attempt, the warlord era (1916-1928), Japan's Twenty-One Demands, and the May Fourth Movement (1919) with its New Culture ideas. Sun reorganised the KMT with Soviet help and formed the First United Front with the CCP. After his death, Chiang Kai-shek led the Northern Expedition (1926-1928), broke with the communists (1927) and established the Nationalist government at Nanjing, nominally unifying China.
section-213: Origins: the CCP was founded in 1921, influenced by the May Fourth Movement and the Russian Revolution. After Chiang's 1927 purge, it shifted to rural bases. Mao developed a peasant-based strategy and guerrilla warfare in the Jiangxi Soviet. The Long March (1934-1935) preserved the party and established Mao's leadership (Zunyi, 1935); Yan'an became the communist base, where the party developed its ideology, organisation and popular support.

War and civil war: the Japanese invasion of Manchuria (1931) and full-scale war (1937) created nationalist sentiment. The Xi'an Incident (1936) led to the Second United Front. The communists gained support through guerrilla resistance against Japan, land reform (rent reduction), disciplined troops and mass mobilisation, while the KMT suffered from corruption, inflation, defeats and dependence on landlords. In the Civil War (1946-1949), decisive battles (Liaoshen, Huaihai, Pingjin) gave the communists victory.

1949 and its significance: Mao proclaimed the PRC on 1 October 1949; the KMT retreated to Taiwan. The revolution ended a century of foreign humiliation, unified the country, and transformed China's society through land reform, collectivisation, nationalisation and women's legal rights. It also brought one-party rule and political campaigns that caused great suffering.
section-214: Great Leap Forward (1958-1962): Mao's attempt to industrialise rapidly through mass mobilisation, people's communes and backyard steel furnaces, rejecting the Soviet model. Unrealistic targets, exaggerated reports, disruption of agriculture and continued grain procurement caused the Great Famine (1959-1961), in which tens of millions died. Peng Dehuai's criticism led to his purge. Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping's recovery policies followed, reducing Mao's influence temporarily.

Cultural Revolution (1966-1976): Mao mobilised Red Guards against party leaders, intellectuals and 'old' culture, purged Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping, closed schools and universities, and sent millions of youth to the countryside. The Gang of Four dominated; factional violence spread; the army restored order; Lin Biao died (1971). Cultural heritage was destroyed, education and the economy suffered, and millions were persecuted. It ended with Mao's death and the arrest of the Gang of Four (1976).

Evaluation: both movements were driven by Mao's utopian vision of rapid transformation and permanent revolution, and his struggle with party rivals. They caused enormous human suffering and economic damage. The CCP's 1981 resolution blamed Mao for the Cultural Revolution while upholding his overall historical role. These experiences shaped Deng's later emphasis on pragmatism, stability and economic development.
section-215: Deng's reforms (from 1978): the Four Modernisations; decollectivisation and the household responsibility system; township and village enterprises; Special Economic Zones (Shenzhen, 1980) and opening to foreign investment; gradual price reform; and 'socialism with Chinese characteristics'. China achieved extraordinary growth, lifting hundreds of millions from poverty. Politically, the party maintained its monopoly of power.

Tiananmen (1989): students and workers demanded political reform and an end to corruption; the government imposed martial law and the army crushed the protests (3-4 June). After this, the party combined continued economic liberalisation (Deng's Southern Tour, 1992) with strict political control and patriotic education. Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) returned to China under 'one country, two systems'.

China in the twenty-first century: WTO membership (2001), becoming the second-largest economy (2010), the Belt and Road Initiative, technological advances and military modernisation have made China a global power. Under Xi Jinping, central control has increased, term limits were removed, and China has become more assertive internationally. Challenges include inequality, an ageing population, environmental problems, slowing growth, human rights criticism (Xinjiang, Hong Kong, Tibet), the Taiwan question and rivalry with the USA and neighbours, including India.
section-218: Northeast India is a meeting point of South Asia, East Asia and Southeast Asia, so its archaeology is important for understanding the movement of people, crops (such as rice), technologies (shouldered celts, cord-marked pottery) and cultural practices (megaliths). Its archaeology is still less developed than other parts of India because of thick forests, heavy rainfall that destroys organic remains, steep terrain, acidic soils, political instability, and limited institutional support.

Key themes include the prehistoric stone-tool traditions, the Neolithic and its links with Southeast Asia, living megalithic traditions among the Khasis, Nagas and others, and the historical archaeology of Kamarupa, the Ahoms, Koches, Chutiyas, Kacharis, Manipur and Tripura. Mizoram has sites such as Vangchhia in Champhai district, with standing stones and carvings, which have been studied by the Archaeological Survey of India.
section-219: Colonial period: early reports by British officers, such as John Lubbock's note on stone tools from the Naga Hills (1867), J. H. Hutton's and J. P. Mills's ethnographic studies, which documented megaliths of the Khasis and Nagas, and P. R. T. Gurdon's work on the Khasis (1907). The Archaeological Survey surveyed historical monuments in Assam (such as at Tezpur and Sivasagar), and Kanaklal Barua and others studied Assamese history.

Postcolonial period: systematic excavations began, for example at Daojali Hading in the North Cachar Hills (Dima Hasao district of Assam, by M. C. Goswami and T. C. Sharma, 1961-1963), Sarutaru near Guwahati, and Ambari in Guwahati. Gauhati University's Department of Anthropology, the North-Eastern Hill University (NEHU) in Shillong and state archaeology departments developed research. Scholars such as T. C. Sharma, Dilip K. Medhi, Manjil Hazarika ('Prehistory and Archaeology of Northeast India', 2017), Tiatoshi Jamir and Pamela Jamir in Nagaland and others have developed the field.
section-220: Culture-historical approaches classified tools and pottery to define cultures and timelines, often assuming that cultural traits spread by diffusion or migration, for example explaining the Northeast Neolithic as derived from Southeast Asia. Processual approaches emphasised environmental adaptation, subsistence and systems (for example, studying how jhum cultivation and settlement patterns related to ecology).

Post-processual and interpretive approaches focus on meanings, symbols and social identities - useful for studying megaliths as markers of memory, status and community. Ethnoarchaeology is particularly important in the Northeast because many communities still practise traditions such as megalith-building, pottery-making, jhum cultivation and weaving, which help interpret archaeological evidence. Postcolonial and indigenous approaches question colonial assumptions and involve communities.
section-221: Palaeolithic tools have been found in the Garo Hills of Meghalaya (the Rongram valley, Ganol and Simsang river valleys), Tripura (Haora and Khowai valleys, where fossil-wood tools were used), Arunachal Pradesh (Kamla valley, Daphabum), Assam and Nagaland. Tools include choppers, handaxes and cleavers, often made of quartzite, dolerite and fossil wood. Their dating is uncertain because of a lack of absolute dates, though they may resemble the Hoabinhian and other Southeast Asian traditions.

Mesolithic and microlithic tools are reported from the Garo Hills (Selbalgiri), Tripura and other places. Some sites in the Garo Hills show a sequence from Palaeolithic to Neolithic. Northeast prehistory is connected both with the Soanian and Acheulian traditions of the subcontinent and with the pebble-tool traditions of Southeast Asia, but more research and dating are needed.
section-222: The Northeast Neolithic is characterised by polished stone tools - especially shouldered celts (axes with shoulders for hafting) and rounded-butt axes - cord-marked and impressed pottery, grinding stones and evidence of cultivation, possibly of rice and other crops. Important sites include Daojali Hading (Dima Hasao, Assam), Sarutaru (Kamrup), Selbalgiri and other sites in the Garo Hills, sites in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills such as Pynthorlangtein, Napchik (Manipur), and sites in Nagaland and Arunachal (Parsi-Parlo).

Its features are similar to Southeast Asian and southern Chinese Neolithic traditions, suggesting connections through migration or exchange, possibly with Austroasiatic-speaking peoples (such as the ancestors of the Khasis). Dates are still debated: some estimates place the Northeast Neolithic between about 3000 and 1000 BCE, later than the Neolithic in western South Asia, and in some areas Neolithic-type tools continued until recent times. The Neolithic is linked with the origins of shifting cultivation and settled villages in the region.
section-223: Megaliths ('big stones') include menhirs (standing stones), dolmens (table stones) and stone circles, erected for burial, commemoration of the dead, feasts of merit and village boundaries. The Northeast is remarkable for living megalithic traditions continuing into modern times. In Meghalaya, the Khasi and Jaintia people erected menhirs (mawbynna) and table stones (mawkynthei) for ancestors; the Nartiang monoliths in the Jaintia Hills include some of the tallest in the region. The Nagas erected stones to commemorate feasts of merit and the dead (such as at Willong Khullen in Manipur). The Dimasa Kacharis' carved stone pillars stand at Kasomari (Dimapur).

In Mizoram, the Vangchhia site in Champhai district has many menhirs, some with carvings of humans, animals and weapons, associated with commemoration and possibly the Thangchhuah feasts; other memorial stones (lungdawh) are found across Mizoram. Scholars compare these traditions with megaliths in Indonesia (Sumba, Nias), Laos (Plain of Jars) and South India, raising questions about connections between South and Southeast Asia.
section-224: Prehistoric people in the Northeast lived by hunting, gathering and fishing in forests and rivers, using stone tools and probably bamboo and wood (which rarely survive). Neolithic communities began cultivating crops - perhaps rice, millet, taro and yams - and domesticating animals like pigs and chickens. Shifting cultivation (jhum), still practised today, probably has prehistoric roots.

Technologies include stone tools (from flaked choppers to polished shouldered celts), pottery (handmade cord-marked wares and later wheel-made wares), bamboo and cane crafts, weaving, iron-working (the Khasi Hills had an important traditional iron-smelting industry, studied at sites near Nongkrem and Mawmluh, possibly dating back over a thousand years) and salt production (salt springs in Nagaland and Manipur). Ethnoarchaeology of present communities helps understand these ancient technologies.
section-225: The Ahoms (1228-1826) left important material remains: the maidams (mound burials) of Ahom kings and nobles at Charaideo (Sivasagar district), sometimes called the 'pyramids of Assam', which were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2024 - the first cultural site of the Northeast on the list. In Sivasagar (Rangpur) and Gargaon: the Rang Ghar (an amphitheatre for royal games, built under Pramatta Singha, often called Asia's oldest surviving amphitheatre), the Talatal Ghar (a multi-storeyed palace with underground floors, built under Rudra Singha and Rajeswar Singha) and the Kareng Ghar at Gargaon.

Temples include the Sivadol, Vishnudol and Devidol at Sivasagar (built by Queen Ambika in the 1730s) and many others. The Ahoms built large tanks (Sivasagar, Joysagar, Gourisagar), roads (Ali) and embankments, and used burnt bricks with a lime-based mortar (with ingredients such as eggs and black gram, according to tradition). Coins, weapons (cannons), manuscripts (buranjis) and copper plate inscriptions add to the evidence.
section-226: Kamarupa (also called Pragjyotisha) was an ancient kingdom in the Brahmaputra valley, mentioned in Samudragupta's Allahabad Pillar inscription (fourth century) as a frontier state. It was ruled by the Varman dynasty (c. 350-650, including Bhaskaravarman), the Mlechchha (Salastambha) dynasty (c. 650-900) and the Pala dynasty (c. 900-1100). Capitals included Pragjyotishpur (Guwahati), Haruppeshwara (Tezpur) and Durjaya.

Archaeological remains: the Da Parbatia door frame near Tezpur (c. fifth-sixth century), carved in the Gupta style with figures of Ganga and Yamuna, is one of the earliest sculptural remains; the ruins of Madan Kamdev (Kamrup), with erotic and religious sculptures (tenth-twelfth centuries); excavations at Ambari in Guwahati, which revealed sculptures, pottery and structures from the seventh to twelfth centuries; Surya Pahar (Goalpara), with rock-cut Hindu, Buddhist and Jain images; and Bamuni Hills at Tezpur. The Kamakhya temple in Guwahati, rebuilt in later centuries, stands on an ancient site.
section-227: The Koch dynasty, founded by Bishwa Singha (c. 1515) in western Assam and north Bengal (Cooch Behar), reached its height under Naranarayana (1540-1586) and his brother and general Chilarai, who conquered large areas. Naranarayana rebuilt the Kamakhya temple (1565) after its destruction, and the Koches patronised Srimanta Sankardeva and Vaishnavism. They issued silver coins (Narayani tanka) and built the Hayagriva Madhava temple at Hajo. The kingdom later split into Koch Bihar and Koch Hajo.

The Chutiya kingdom ruled eastern Assam and parts of Arunachal (Sadiya) from about the twelfth or thirteenth century until it was conquered by the Ahoms in 1523-1524. Remains associated with them include the Tamreswari temple (the 'copper temple') near Sadiya, Bhismaknagar fort near Roing (Arunachal Pradesh), with brick structures, and the Malinithan temple site at Likabali (Arunachal), with sculptures from around the thirteenth-fourteenth centuries. Students should note that some attributions are debated.
section-228: Rock art includes paintings (pictographs) and engravings (petroglyphs) on rock surfaces. In the Northeast, rock art is less studied than in central India (Bhimbetka), but examples have been reported in Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Assam, Manipur and Mizoram; they include engravings of human figures, animals, weapons and geometric designs. The rock-cut relief sculptures of Unakoti in Tripura (seventh-ninth centuries or later), including huge carved faces of Shiva and other deities, are a major site of rock-cut art, though religious and historical rather than prehistoric.

Dating and interpretation of rock art are difficult; archaeologists study its style, context, weathering and local traditions. In Mizoram, carvings on stones at sites such as Vangchhia show human figures and animals, linked with memorial traditions. Rock art provides evidence of symbolic thought, belief and social life.
section-229: Kamarupa inscriptions include the Umachal rock inscription of Surendravarman (fifth century, in Guwahati), the earliest inscription found in Assam; the Nagajari-Khanikargaon inscription; the Doobi and Nidhanpur copper plates of Bhaskaravarman, which give the genealogy of the Varman kings; the Tezpur rock inscription of Harjaravarman (829 CE) and copper plates of the Pala kings. Most are in Sanskrit, using the Gupta-derived script, and record land grants and royal genealogies.

Ahom inscriptions include copper plates, stone inscriptions in temples and coins with legends in Ahom script, Sanskrit and Assamese, together with the buranjis (chronicles). Koch inscriptions include the Kamakhya temple inscription of Naranarayana (1565) and coins. Epigraphy helps reconstruct dynasties, land grants, religion, administration and the spread of Sanskrit culture in the region.
section-230: Buddhist remains in the Northeast include the Pilak site in southern Tripura (eighth-twelfth centuries), with terracotta plaques and Buddhist and Hindu sculptures, showing links with the Buddhist art of Bengal and Myanmar; Boxanagar (Tripura) with Buddhist stupa remains; and Surya Pahar in Goalpara (Assam), with rock-cut images and votive stupas. In Arunachal Pradesh and Sikkim, Tibetan Buddhist monasteries such as Tawang (founded in 1680-1681) and Rumtek have murals, thangka paintings and sculptures.

Hiuen Tsang's account mentions that Buddhism was less prominent in Kamarupa, though the king respected Buddhist scholars. Buddhist art of the region shows connections with Pala art of Bengal, Tibetan traditions and Southeast Asian (Burmese) styles. Students should refer to the prescribed readings for specific cave art sites included in the syllabus.
section-231: Postcolonial archaeology critiques the colonial legacy in research: colonial scholars often viewed Northeast communities as 'primitive' and 'unchanging', interpreted their past through diffusion from outside, and focused on monuments associated with Sanskritic or Ahom states while ignoring hill communities. Colonial collecting also removed artefacts to museums abroad.

Postcolonial approaches aim to write regional histories from local perspectives, recognise the agency and complexity of hill and valley societies, question the categories of 'tribe' and 'civilisation', examine how archaeology has been used in nation-building and identity politics, and address the repatriation of objects (such as Naga human remains held in Oxford's Pitt Rivers Museum, which began to be discussed with Naga communities in the 2020s).
section-232: Indigenous archaeology involves indigenous communities in the research process and respects their knowledge, values and rights. It recognises oral traditions, genealogies, place names and traditional knowledge as valuable sources of history, and seeks to make archaeology serve community interests, such as cultural revival and identity. It also respects sacred sites and objects.

In the Northeast, where many communities have strong oral traditions and living practices (such as megalith-building and jhum), indigenous archaeology is especially relevant. Examples include research in Nagaland by Naga archaeologists (Tiatoshi Jamir) working with village communities, and the documentation of village histories and migration sites. This approach can reduce suspicion of outsiders and produce more accurate interpretations.
section-233: In the Northeast, land is often owned by communities, clans or chiefs under customary law, and protected by the Sixth Schedule, Article 371A (Nagaland), 371G (Mizoram) and others. Archaeological sites and evidence of past settlement can be used to support claims of ancestral territory, indigenous status or historical rights in boundary disputes between states and communities.

At the same time, designating sites as protected monuments under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act (1958) can restrict local land use, creating conflicts. Development projects (dams, roads, mining) may destroy sites, requiring heritage impact assessments. Archaeologists must therefore consider how their work affects public policy, land rights and community interests, and avoid their findings being misused in ethnic conflicts.
section-234: Human remains are especially sensitive. Many Northeast communities have specific beliefs about the dead, ancestors and burial sites. During the colonial period, human skulls and remains (including Naga trophy skulls) were collected and taken to museums in Britain and elsewhere without consent. Today, ethical guidelines require informed consent from communities, respect for remains, careful handling, limited destructive analysis and the possibility of reburial or repatriation.

Scientific analysis of remains, including DNA and isotopes, can provide valuable information about ancestry, migration, diet and health, but must be conducted responsibly and shared with the communities. International principles include the Vermillion Accord on Human Remains (World Archaeological Congress, 1989) and UNESCO guidelines. In India, there is a need for clearer laws and protocols.
section-235: Collaborative or community archaeology involves local people at every stage - planning, excavation, interpretation, conservation and presentation. Benefits include access to local knowledge (oral history, traditional names, uses of land), better protection of sites by communities, greater trust, skill development and employment, and interpretations that reflect local perspectives. Community museums and heritage festivals can present the results.

Examples in the Northeast include village-based heritage projects in Nagaland and Meghalaya, collaboration between universities and village councils, and the involvement of local youth in surveys. Collaboration also requires respecting community decisions about sensitive sites and sharing benefits such as tourism income.
section-236: Future directions include: more systematic surveys and excavations, especially in less explored areas such as Mizoram, Arunachal and Tripura; scientific dating (radiocarbon, luminescence) to build reliable chronologies; archaeobotany to study early agriculture, including the origins of rice cultivation; ancient DNA studies to understand population history and links with Southeast and East Asia; and remote sensing to locate sites under forest cover.

Other needs include protecting sites threatened by development, climate change and looting; developing museums and heritage tourism; training local archaeologists; integrating archaeology with oral traditions and ethnography; and connecting Northeast archaeology to global debates about migration, agriculture, megalithic traditions and state formation. The region's position between South, East and Southeast Asia makes its archaeology of global importance.
section-238: Introduction: the Northeast's geography (hills, forests, high rainfall, rivers), cultural diversity and position between South and Southeast Asia shape its archaeology. Research began with colonial reports and ethnography (Lubbock, Hutton, Mills, Gurdon), followed by postcolonial excavations (Daojali Hading, Sarutaru, Ambari) and university research (Gauhati University, NEHU). Theoretical approaches include culture history, processual archaeology, interpretive and ethnoarchaeological approaches, and postcolonial and indigenous perspectives.

Prehistory: Palaeolithic tools from the Garo Hills (Rongram valley), Tripura (fossil wood tools), Arunachal and Assam; Mesolithic microliths in the Garo Hills; and a Neolithic with shouldered celts, polished axes and cord-marked pottery (Daojali Hading, Sarutaru, Selbalgiri, Khasi and Jaintia sites, Napchik in Manipur), with strong links to Southeast Asia and southern China. Dating remains a major problem.

Megalithic cultures: living traditions among the Khasis, Jaintias (Nartiang), Nagas, Dimasas (Kasomari pillars) and Mizos (Vangchhia), erected for the dead, feasts of merit and commemoration, comparable with Southeast Asian megaliths. Subsistence and technology: hunting-gathering, shifting cultivation, early rice and tuber cultivation, pottery, iron-smelting in the Khasi Hills and salt production. These show adaptation to a forested, hilly environment.
section-239: Kamarupa: an early historical kingdom (fourth-twelfth centuries) under the Varman, Salastambha and Pala dynasties; remains include the Da Parbatia door frame, Madan Kamdev, Ambari, Surya Pahar and Bamuni Hills; inscriptions include the Umachal rock inscription, the Nidhanpur and Doobi copper plates and the Tezpur inscription. These show the spread of Sanskritic religion and kingship in the region.

Ahoms (1228-1826): the maidams of Charaideo (UNESCO World Heritage, 2024), the Rang Ghar, Talatal Ghar and Kareng Ghar, the Sivadol temples, tanks, roads and embankments, coins and buranjis. Koches: Naranarayana's rebuilding of Kamakhya (1565), the Hajo temples and Narayani coins. Chutiyas: the Tamreswari temple, Bhismaknagar fort and Malinithan. Other kingdoms include the Kacharis (Dimapur and Maibang ruins), the Jaintia kingdom and Tripura (Udaipur temples).

Art and inscriptions: rock art and engravings (including Vangchhia carvings in Mizoram), rock-cut reliefs at Unakoti (Tripura), Buddhist remains at Pilak (Tripura) and Surya Pahar, and Tibetan Buddhist monastery art (Tawang). Epigraphy from Kamarupa, Ahom and Koch contexts helps reconstruct political and cultural history. Together, these materials show that Northeast India had complex states, religious traditions and artistic achievements, connected with both Bengal and Southeast Asia.
section-240: Postcolonial and indigenous approaches: they question colonial views of Northeast communities as primitive and isolated, criticise the neglect of hill societies, address the repatriation of objects and human remains taken in colonial times, and give importance to oral traditions and local knowledge. They emphasise community participation and respect for sacred sites.

Public policy, land rights and ethics: archaeological evidence can be used in claims for ancestral land and identity and in boundary disputes, while heritage protection can restrict local land use. Development projects threaten sites. Ethical issues include treatment of human remains (consent, reburial, repatriation), responsible scientific analysis, and avoiding misuse of archaeology in ethnic politics.

Collaboration and future: collaborative research with village councils and communities improves interpretation and conservation; the future requires more surveys, scientific dating, archaeobotany, ancient DNA, remote sensing, local training, museums and heritage management. Responsible, locally engaged and scientifically careful archaeology can reveal the Northeast's significant role in Asian history, including the spread of agriculture, megalithic traditions and state formation.
